questions.question:
Will the Minister for Defence be pleased to state:
a) why airlines have raised ticket prices by 15-30% across domestic and international routes
as jet fuel rates surged to 150-200 dollars per barrel from 85-90 dollars, with the Middle
East conflict driving up operational costs at a time when Pakistan's aviation sector was
already struggling to recover from previous crises;
b) whether the Iran war has sparked fears of a deep travel slump and widespread grounding
of planes, with carriers facing soaring insurance premiums, rerouting costs, and
weakened passenger demand; and
c) what contingency measures exist to prevent mass layoffs or collapse of domestic carriers,
particularly Pakistan International Airlines, which was already operating with a fleet of
just 20 functional aircraft out of 31; and
d) what fuel hedging mechanisms or tariff relief is being considered to prevent the sector's
complete destabilization ?
questions.reply:
(a) PIA Response: PIA along with other
airlines (throughout the world) were forced to escalate prices / fuel surcharges to cover the operational
costs due to high fuel prices. However, even with these measures, PIA and other Pakistani earners are
still facing severe challenges to meet even the operational costs.

AIR S1AI/S Response:
The current geopolitical situation in the Gulf region, including tensions involving Iran and the
United States, has further intensified existing cost pressures on the aviation sector. In this context, the

increase in air ticket prices, both in the international and domestic market has not been fully aligned
with the sharp rise in jet fuel costs.
Globally, jet fuel prices have increased by approximately 55-105%, whereas in Pakistan the
domestic jet fuel price has risen by more than 150%. As a result, the fuel component of operating costs
has significantly shifted, increasing from around 30-35% of total operating costs previously to
approximately 50-55% at present.
In addition to cost escalation, market dynamics have also played a key role. The induction of
additional capacity by one of private carrier has resulted in excess supply in the domestic and
international market, intensifying competition among carriers. Consequently, airlines have been
operating under constrained pricing flexibility and have been unable to fully pass on the increased fuel
cost burden to passengers, In order to retain market share in an already highly competitive environment

AIR BLUE’S Response:
The ongoing regional tensions between Iran and the United States have significantly impacted
global fuel prices, with aviation fuel in Pakistan increasing from approximately PKR 160 to around
PKR 400 which shows an increase of 180 %. This sharp escalation has substantially raised airline
operating costs, as fuel constitutes a major component of overall flight expenses.
Historically, fuel accounted for nearly 30% of total costs; however, this proportion has now surged
to approximately 60%, placing considerable financial strain on airline operations and challenging
economic viability.
Airblue has recently shared its domestic operations data with the Pakistan Civil Aviation Authority,
presenting a comparative analysis of seat factors for the period 1st
April to 25th April 2025 versus the
same period in 2026. The data reflects a decline in seat factor from 91% in 2025 to 690 in 2026,
indicating demand compression and reduced passenger purchasing power on primary domestic routes.
As a result, the airline implemented fare increases and partially passed on these costs to passengers
however, as reflected in the data shared above, this led to a decline in seat factor.
The average domestic fare on these key routes for the full month of April 2025 was approximately
PKR 28,000. However, During the latter part of April 2026, fares on these routes were reduced to as
low as PKR 10,000, resulting in average fares across flights falling approximately PKR '15,000. This
decline in average fares towards the end of April 2026 reflects prevailing market conditions, wherein
excess capacity introduced into the domestic market, particularly by one airline, combined with
relatively subdued demand, intensified competition and exerted downward pressure on fares, resulting
in decrease in revenues.
As a result of these combined factors, escalating fuel costs and reduced revenues, airlines are
facing significant financial losses, making current operations increasingly unsustainable.

(b) PIA’s Response:
The conflict has severely impacted the regional aviation industry with daily costs exceeding
US$600 million, jet fuel prices rising nearly 84% since February 28, 2026, and a 66% drop in
passenger traffic at Dubai International Airport in March.

Air Sial’s Response:
The situation in the Middle East, particularly involving tensions linked to Iran, continues to
generate uncertainty in regional aviation operations. This has led to increased operational costs,
including higher fuel cost, premiums and extended routings in certain sectors due to restricted airspace
usage and underutilization of its fleet As a result, airlines are under additional financial losses across
both international and domestic networks.
Furthermore, the regional developments have contributed to subdued passenger demand and
reduced travel activity on impacted corridors On UAE routes m particular. Pakistani airlines are
operating under significant constraints due to unilateral slot cancellations, and short-term weekly
capacity approvals by the UAE aeronautical authorities. The limits advance flight planning, weakens

booking visibility, and places pressure on fare stability and overall management.

Air Bluel’s Response:
Due to the ongoing regional conflict, passenger demand has declined significantly resulting in a-
slowdown in overall travel activity. Airspace closures ave e widespread cancellations, particularly
across the UAE sector.
To ensure safety, airlines are operating on extended routings to avoid conflicted trcas, which has
further increased operating time and costs consequently, less than 50% of scheduled flight to currently
operation with a number of aircraft grounded due to reduced demand and operational constrains.
Specifically operations to the UAE remain limited under the current circumstances as slot approvals
have not been granted in line with the full scheduled plan, further restricting operational capacity.

(c) PIA’s response:
While the current geopolitical environment presents an undeniable challenge, the risk of abrupt
collapse or mass layoffs is being mitigated through a combination of privatization, financial
restructuring, operational adjustments, and policy support mechanisms. The focus remains on
stabilization and gradual transformation, rather than emergency downsizing.

Air Sials response:
Airlines are currently managing the prevailing situation through a combination of operational and
financial adjustments, absorption of additional costs from internal resources. However, these measures
are essentially short-term in nature and may not remain sufficient to sustain long-term operations if
existing cost pressures and structural constraints Persist.

Air blue’s response:
Air Blue is currently striving to absorb the additional operational costs through its internal
resources. However, if the situation persists for an extended period it will have a detrimental impact on
the overall viability of airline operations, particularly affecting domestic services and Hajj operations.

(d) PIA’s response:
A collaborative approach combining limited fuel hedging and targeted tariff relief is being pursued
to mitigate the immediate impact of fuel price volatility, with the objective of preventing financial
destabilization while maintaining operational continuity across aviation sector.

Air Sial’s response:
Fuel hedging mechanisms remain largely underdeveloped in Pakistan. Airlines currently do not
have the capacity to meaningfully hedge fuel exposure. In this context, policy-level support measures,
including rationalization or subsidy of jet fuel prices, are critical to ensure operational sustainability.
Furthermore, consideration may be given to the introduction of a controlled and demand-aligned
capacity framework on both domestic and international routes in Hn^th actual passenger traffic trends.
In addition, the immediate withdraw of applicable GST on domestic aviation fuel and the import of
spare parts is strongly recommended, as these continue to place a substantial burden on already
strained operating costs.

Air Blue’s response:
Global crude oil prices increased by approximately 50-100% during the recent crisis however,
domestic jet fuel prices in Pakistan have increased by over 150% indicating the impact of additional
pricing components beyound crude trends, Furthermore, as a majority of let fuel used by Pakistani
airlines is refined locally from imported crude, this divergence highlights the need to review the ex-
refinery pricing mechanism and its linkage to international benchmarks. center

and its linkage to international benchmarks.
It is imperative for the Government to undertake the following measures:
1. Rationalization and reduction of jet fuel prices. nasseneers

2. Reduction in FBR-imposed taxes, including reason of FED P * across all Gulf sectors.
3. Removal of GST on aircraft and spare parts for all airlines, in relief currently extended to PIA.
Note: Fly Jinnah has not provided any response to above queries. Serene Air currently non-
operational , the response is not applicable.

(b) The criteria for issuance of Air Service Licenses are comprehensively stipulated in the
applicable Air Navigation orders (Nos), which are promulgated and updated periodically by PCAA.
These ANOs outline detailed regulatory requirements encompassing financial soundness, operational
capability, safety compliance, and organizational structure.
A new ANO is also under process. However, a comprehensive evaluation checklist is available on
the official website of PCAA. This checklist requires applicants to undergo rigorous financial
assessment, demonstrate adequate operational preparedness, and meet all prescribed safety and

regulatory standards. Licenses are granted only after thorough scrutiny and satisfactory fulfillment of
all applicable requirements.

(c) As per the provisions of the National Aviation Policy 2023, Air Service License holders are
required to obtain an Air Operator Certificate (AOC) within a period of three (03) years from the date
of issuance of the license. The commencement of commercial flight operations is contingent upon the
successful acquisition of the Air Operator Certificate (AOC). Accordingly, Air Service License holders
are expected to initiate their operations upon completion of all regulatory requirements and subsequent
issuance of the AOC within the stipulated timeframe.

(d) It is submitted that commercial flight operation in Pakistan is governed under the provisions
of Pakistan Civil Aviation Act, 2023 (the Act) and National Aviation Policy, 2023 (the policy). In
order to fully comprehend the airline pricing following are submitted for consideration:

Airfare Mechanism
As for the (fares) charged by the airlines for supply of air services, liberalization and allowing
market forces to determine fares is the international best practice, which the Policy also endorses under
Para 1.6.1 clause (6) ibid prescribing therein that “airfares will be determined through market forces of
supply and demand”.
Monopolistic practices (if any) can all be discouraged through fair competition and encouraging
new market entrants which in Pakistan is ensured through PCA Act, 2023 and NAP-2023. With
regards to cartelization and other such anti- competitive practices, the Competition Commission of
Pakistan (CCP) being the relevant forum actively monitors the aviation sector to detect and penalize
anti- competitive practices.
While affordability of air travel is one aspect; it is equally important to consider the characteristic
of aviation business. Airlines are for-profit entities liable to pay taxes and duties. Flight operations
and/or ticket—pricing on a particular route or routes Is an airline’s commercial decision, which is
significantly dependent upon various factors including passenger demand, load-factors based on its
aircraft fleet, compatibility of its aircraft with available airport infrastructure, operational costs,
regulatory compliances, etc. Yet, there is n guarantee for the airline that all its capacity would get
sold on all its flight. Globally, airlines use Revenue-Management System (RMS), which factors in
demand,
Capacity, cost, competition, booking time etc. to calculate fares in real time. RIMS automatically
adjust air fares depending said factors. The current Revenue Management System being used by
Pakistani Airlines is based on the market forces of demand and supply and naturally market forces
are considered nondiscriminatory.

Airline Pricing Strategy
An airlines pricing strategic conform to supply and demand at a particular point in time, and in
multiple occasions, operators arc compelled to sell air-tickcts below cost or operating the aircraft and
recoup incurred loss at some other point. As observed over time, average airfares have generally
remained within appropriate ranges.

Airfare Variations
Considering the dynamics of Aviation, tickets purchased on short notice (usually with a gap of 1-3
days) are expensive owing to either scarcity of supply or increased with a gap and demand. Whereas,
for air-travel planned well in advance the ticket prices are usually very stable and significantly lower in
comparison with last minute bookings.

(e) The Government, through enforcement of the Pakistan Civil Aviation Authority (PCAA)
regulations, ensures compliance with aviation safety standards and operational readiness prior to the
commencement of airline services through a comprehensive and structured regulatory oversight

framework.
These aviation safety standards (PCAA regulations) covers subjects of operational flight safety,
cabin safety, ground safety, cargo safety, aircraft airworthiness, aviation security, personnel licensing
and aeromedical. It also includes a number of specialized subjects within broad faculties.
These regulations are required to be implemented by the airline/service provider and PCAA
ensures adherence to these, through layers of monitoring activities involving Certification Audits,
Surveillance Inspections Ramp Inspections, Inspections and practical activity (drills) monitoring.
ICAO has issued Effective Implementation of Pakistan in 2024 at 84/59%, which indicates that Civil
Aviation System is in compliance with ICAO SARPs for Critical Elements (CE).
No airline is permitted to commence operations unless it has successfully completed the Air
Operator Certificate (AOC) certification process, which includes a rigorous evaluation of the
operator’s organizational structure, operational systems, safety management framework, training
programs, and technical readiness, in accordance with applicable national regulations which are based
on ICA Standards and Recommended Practices (SARPs).
The certification process includes detailed review and approval of Operations Manuals, Security
Manuals, Ground Handling, Continuous Airworthiness Management System and associated
procedures; also screening and approval of key accountable personnel, including post holders
responsible for flight assurance; verification and approval of training programs, syllabi, instructors,
training equipment, and facilities; oversight of critical training domains including Crew Resource
Management (CRM), Human Factors, and Safety and Emergency Procedures (SEP); assessment of
Safety Management aircraft, equipment, and operational control systems; and conduct of
demonstration and proving flights prior to issuance of the AOC. Following certification, continuous
surveillance oversight is ensured through surveillance inspection program, including regular
inspections at operator bases and outstations; this inspection include en-route cockpit and cabin
inspections to monitor real-time operational compliance; ramp inspections, including those conducted
in line with internationally recognized Safety Assessment of Foreign Aircraft (SAFA) principles, to
verify aircraft condition, documentation, crew compliance, and operational readiness; continuous
oversight of training and checking activities, including monitoring of instructors, simulator sessions,
and recurrent training programs ongoing review and approval of manuals and revisions to ensure
alignment with regulatory updates and international standards; monitoring of Flight Data Monitoring
(FDM), occurrence reporting systems, and safety performance monitoring. The PCAA regulatory
framework is also continuously reviewed and updated with latest amendments in ICAO SARPs and
global best practices, ensuring that Pakistan’s aviation system remains aligned with recognized
international regulatory safety standards. Regulatory non-compliance or deviation is not tolerated and a
finding is raised depending on the level of non-compliance and related safety risk. No operator is
allowed to continue a particular activity/operation in case a level one finding is found during

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Interior and Narcotics Control be pleased to state the steps being
taken by the Government to strengthen law enforcement agencies to curb the increasing
Cyber Crimes in the country?
questions.reply:
To
address the increasing threat of digital crimes, the Government of Pakistan has shifted from a reactive
to a more proactive and institutionalized approach. The Government has taken the following steps to
curb the cybercrime focusing on legislative reform, specialized agency formation, and international
collaboration.

1. Establishment of National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA)
In a major institutional overhaul, the government has replaced the Federal Investigation
Agency's (FIA) Cyber Crime Wing with a more specialized body, the NCCIA, in 2025.
Enhanced Autonomy: The NCCIA has been granted independent authority to investigate and
prosecute cybercrime cases.
Forensic Capabilities: The Agency is equipped with modern digital forensic laboratories
capable of handling complex cases involving encrypted data, social media offences, and financial
fraud.
Enforcement:
Operational Statistics(2023-2026)
1 2 3 4 5 6
S.N Registered 2023 2024 2025 2026
1 Complaints 134710 161828 157465 77023
2 Verification 82396 108989 141681 58286
3 Enquiries 18012 24012 30214 8048
4 Cases 1375 1667 2256 457
5 Accused Arrested 2007 2157 2916 520
6 Convictions 92 60 39 8
7 Acquittals 416 268 168 25

2. Legislative Strengthening: PÉCA Amendments 2025

The Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA), 2016 was amended in 2025 to address
emerging cyber threats, including deep fakes and large- scale misinformation.
1. Establishment of the Social Media Protection Regulatory Authority (SMPRA) to ensure platf
compliance and timely removal of unlawful content.
2. Creation of Social Media Protection Tribunals comprising legal, technical, and media experts
to ensure efficient and technically sound adjudication of cases.
3. Introduction of Section 26-A to penalize deliberate spread of false information causing public
panic, with punishment of up to three years' imprisonment.
3. National Cyber Security Policy (NCSP) Implementation
The Government is implementing the National Cyber Security Policy, recognizing cyber threats as
a matter of national security.
1. Establishment of a centralized National Cyber Emergency Response Team to monitor, report,
and mitigate cyber threats targeting critical infrastructure, including energy and financial
sectors.
2. Mandatory localization of sensitive data for critical sectors such as identity management,
finance, and defense to minimize risks associated with cross-border data breaches.

3. Specialized Training and Awareness Efforts are underway to enhance the technical capacity of
law enforcement agencies and promote public awareness.
i. Law enforcement personnel are receiving training in advanced areas such as artificial
intelligence-based threat detection and block chain analysis, in collaboration with
international partners.
ii. The NCCIA conducts regular awareness campaigns through social media, seminars, and
workshops to promote digital hygiene and prevent cyber offences such as phishing and
online harassment.

questions.question:

a) whether it is a fact that despite new regulations, governance issues in sports federations
persist; if so, reasons; and
b) whether any federation has been penalized under the new Code of Governance; if so,
details?
questions.reply:
(a) Yes, certain governance issues continue to
persist in some National Sports Federations (NSFs) mainly due to limited institutional capacity to
adopt modern governance practices. National Sports Federations attempt to shield under the pretext of
autonomy and reference to international bodies such as the International Olympic Committee (IOC)
and respective international federations. However, after detailed study of international best practices,
Pakistan Sports Board (PSB) has established a comprehensive regulatory framework, including the
Pakistan Code of Ethics and Governance in Sports, an independent adjudication mechanism, and the
National Sports Federations (Tenure) Rules, 2025, to ensure transparency, accountability, and good
governance. PSB continues to actively enforce these measures through monitoring, engagement, and
corrective actions.

(b)Yes, strict enforcement actions have been taken under the new governance framework.
These include:
1. Directions to National Sports Federations to rectify tenure violations in accordance with the
National Sports Federations (Tenure) Rules, 2025 which restrict the office bearer to a
maximum two tenures of four years on same post as well as maximum age limit of 70
years, leading to compliance by several federations including Karate, Baseball, Taekwondo,
Judo, Basketball, and Sailing;
2. Issuance of warnings and corrective directives in governance and electoral matters; and
3. Decisions through the adjudication mechanism. In addition, disciplinary actions have been
taken in specific cases, including:

offered at revised/new rates;
e) if so, the complete details thereof?
questions.reply:
(a) As
per report of Society the project “Dream Heights” was launched in 2015 for construction of residential
apartments as an affordable housing scheme for IBECHS members through a 20-year installment plan.

(b) As per report of Society not all but a sizable number of members 45-50% are depositing
their monthly installments regularly since September 2015 under the approved 20-year plan. The total
amount deposited by members up to 28th April 2026 is Rs. 6.169 billion. The grey structure of
approximately 1101 apartments have been completed successfully. Total so far the cost for land and
construction of 1101 apartments is calculated as Rs.7 billion approximately. It is worth while to
mention that payments on purchase of land and construction of flats are made in parallel to the
construction company / land owners therefore, deposited amount cannot be accumulated for interest
purpose and the interest credited on the available amount is merged in principal amount/transactions
As per report of Society up to April 2026, the grey structure of 1101 apartments has been
completed. The remaining work mainly pertains to finishing, external development and allied services.
Overall, approximately 60% work has been completed, while around 40% work is still pending.

(c) It is pertinent to mention that initially, 7,043 apartments were booked, 3,429 members
converted their apartments into residential plots on their return consent as approved in AGM /
Registrar. Till April 2026, total number of plots 3,612 apartments remain active out of which
installments of around 1,503 apartments (about 50%) are being received regularly. Members beyond
1101 numbers will be considered for allotment of apartments on construction or alternative of
apartments with their consent/ approval of AGM.

The project is based on a 20-year payment plan, therefore, the possession of grey structured
apartments is tentatively planned to be handed over to the members as early as possible / well before
20 years’ plan subject to favorable conditions pertaining to receipt of installments regularly and
reduction in cost of construction material.

(d) As per report of Society the Society, through Circular No. IBECHS/GDH/2023 dated
11-10-2024, conveyed the members that those whose names are drawn in the balloting for possession
will be required to pay at revised rates due to a 400%–500% increase in construction material costs and
the revision of apartment sizes. The Society cannot afford the whole financial burden alone due to
recent recession in real estate in Pakistan, therefore, different options have been considered, including
partial cost-sharing by members, subject to approval in the upcoming Annual General Meeting. It is
further clarified that this circular is not conclusive and policies may be revised over time to ensure
maximum benefit to the members living within the resources.

(e) As already mentioned at Sr. No. (d) above.

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Planning, Development and Special Initiative be pleased to state:
a) whether it is a fact that Applied Engineering and Emerging Technologies University at
Sambrial (Sialkot), a joint project of the Federal Government and the Government of Punjab
with a cost of Rs. 17 Billion was started in 2020 and was to be completed in 2024, but the project
has remained incomplete and stopped due to non-release of funds by the Federal Government;
and
b) whether the Government of Punjab has released its share of funds; if so, the reasons due to
which the Federal Government has not released funds?
questions.reply:
(a) The project titled "Establishment of University of Applied Engineering and Emerging Technologies
(UAEET), Sialkot" was cleared by the Provincial Development Working Party (PDWP), Government
of the Punjab, in its meeting held on 20.04.2021 and recommended to CDWP at a total cost of Rs.
16,648.47 million (Capital: Rs. 4,673.74 million; Revenue: Rs.11,974.73 million). The Central
Development Working Party (CDWP), in its meeting dated 24.05.2021, recommended the project to
ECNEC, which approved the project on 04.06.2021 at the same cost, with 50% cost sharing between
the Federal Government and the Government of Punjab. The approved gestation period of the project
is 96 months (ending December, 2028); therefore, the project is not due for completion in 2024.

The project is being implemented by the Government of Punjab through Infrastructure
Development Authority Punjab (1DAP). Although, the project was included in PSDP 2021-22 with an
allocation of Rs. 1,500.00 million, however, funds were not released under the Federal share, and the
project has not been included in PSDP thereafter. However, the project has not been formally stopped
and continues to be reflected in the Provincial ADP.

(b) The Government of Punjab has been releasing funds for the project from its own resources.
An amount of approximately Rs. 3,169.785 million has been spent on the project up to June, 2025,
while an allocation of Rs. 100.00 million has been made in ADP 2025-26. As regards the Federal
share, allocations under PSDP are subject to overall resource availability and sectoral priorities
determined by the Federal Government. Due to fiscal constraints and competing demands, the project
could not be accommodated in subsequent PSDPs after 2021-22. Due to fiscal pressures overall PSDP
has been severely curtailed resulting in lack of additional resources.

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Finance and Revenue be pleased to state:
a) whether it is a fact that GST and withholding tax on savings, utilities, and other essential
services have recently been increased; if so, details and reasons thereof;
b) whether the Government has assessed the impact of these increased taxes on inflation,
prices of daily-use items, households expenses and purchasing power of the common people;
c) if so, details thereof along with additional revenue expected to be collected from the tax
increases during the current Financial Year,

d) how will this revenue will be utilized; and
e) the steps taken by the government to reduce the financial burden on the public, control
inflation, and provide relief, especially to middle and low income groups?
questions.reply:
(a) Through the
Finance Act, 2025, certain amendments have been introduced in the withholding tax regime, including
revision ol rates under section 151 relating to profit on debt, along with rationalization of rates under
selected provisions. Under the amended framework, the rate of tax deduction under section 151 has
been increased from 15% to 20% on certain saving instruments and bank deposits. Keeping in view the
international best practices, this enhancement has been made to remove distortions between the
taxation of profit on debt and other heads of income, and to align and rationalize it with the applicable
tax rates tor business income and salaried individuals. Moreover, there is no change in the standard
GST rate has been made through the Finance Act, 2025, and the rate remains at 18% on utilities and
other essential services under the Sales Tax Act,1990.

(b) Additional revenue generated from these measures is credited to the Federal Consolidated
Fund and is utilized by the Federal Government in accordance with constitutional and legal provisions.
These resources support public expenditure on service delivery, infrastructure development, and debt
servicing, as well as transfers to provinces under the National Finance Commission Award.
Collectively, these allocations contribute to economic stability and the overall welfare of the public.

(c) No significant additional revenue is expected from this change, as returns on bank deposits
have declined due to a reduction in profit rates on savings accounts. Consequently, the overall taxable
income from such deposits has decreased, offsetting the impact of the higher withholding tax rate.

(d) There has been no change in the standard rate of General Sales Tax (GST), which continues
to remain at 18% under the Sales Tax Act, 1990. Accordingly, no direct inflationary impact arises from
any adjustment in GST rates. On the income tax side, measures introduced were primarily aimed at
improving horizontal equity. In this regard, income from profit on debt has been aligned with the
applicable tax rates on other heads of income under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. This adjustment
constitutes a redistribution measure and does not directly affect the pricing of goods or services.
Furthermore, through the Finance Act 2025, targeted relief has been provided to salaried and middle-
income taxpayers. This includes rationalization of tax slabs and reductions in effective tax rates,
thereby supporting disposable incomes and mitigating financial pressures on households. Overall, the
recent tax measures are structured to enhance equity and provide relief, without introducing cost-push
factors that would directly contribute to inflation in essential commodities.

(e) The Government, through the Finance Act 2025, has provided targeted relief to salaried and
middle-income taxpayers under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. Tax slabs for salaried individuals
have been rationalized to reduce effective rates. The surcharge under section 4AB has been reduced
from 10% to 9% for salaried individuals, while the super tax slabs under section 4C have been
rationalized to ensure higher contribution from top earners only. Additionally, the tax under section
236K on purchase of property has been reduced, easing the compliance and financial burden on
taxpayers. These measures collectively enhance progressivity and provide meaningful relief to middle-
and low-income groups.

(a) The Capital
Value Tax (CVT) is governed by the provisions of section 8 of Finance Act, 2022, as amended from
time to time. The said Act provides the legal basis for levy, collection and enforcement of CVT on
specified assets. Under this framework, CVT is chargeable on the value of certain assets, including
foreign assets of resident persons and specified motor vehicles, at the prescribed rates. The tax is
administered by the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) and is collected and enforced through the
existing machinery of the income tax law, including provisions relating to filing, assessment, recovery
and appeals. Further, rules and procedures have been notified to operationalize the levy, including
valuation mechanisms, declaration requirements and modes of payment.

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Planning, Development and Special Initiative be pleased to state:
a) whether it is a fact that Pakistan's investment to GDP ratio declined from 15.6% in year-
2022 to around 13.8% in year-2025, remaining significantly below regional peers; if so, the
reasons thereof; and
b) details of concrete policy measures being taken by the Government to raise investment to
GDP ratio and promote export oriented investment and Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), in the
country?
questions.reply:
(a) Pakistan's investment-to-GDP ratio declined from 15.6% in FY2022 to 14.3% in FY2025, primarily
due to challenging macroeconomic conditions. These included the devastating 2022 floods, the Russia-
Ukraine conflict, and the global commodity super-cycle, all of which contributed to elevated inflation
(29.2% in FY2023 and 23.4% in FY2024) and high policy rates (22% in June 2023). Consequently, the
cost of financing increased, constraining private investment. However, the situation is now improving:
the investment- to-GDP ratio rose to 14.3% in FY2025 (revised), up from 13.2% in FY2024, reflecting
gradual macroeconomic stabilization.

(b) The Government is pursuing a comprehensive reform agenda to raise the investment-to-
GDP ratio, anchored in export-led growth, macroeconomic stability, and private sector development
under the 13th Five-Year Plan (2024-29) and URAAN Pakistan framework. Key initiatives include
regulatory simplification under the Asaan Karobar Act, establishment of a „ one-window Business
Facilitation Centre, and measures to deepen financial markets and support SMEs.

At the same time, investment is being promoted through infrastructure development, public-
private partnerships, and industrial expansion under SEZs and CPEC Phase-II. Focus on export-led
growth, sectoral diversification, digital transformation, and skills development is expected to improve
productivity and attract both domestic and foreign investment.

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Commerce be pleased to state what strategy is being evolved to formulate a
comprehensive national export strategy coupled with proactive trade policy to enhance
Pakistan's global competitiveness, diversify export destinations and strengthen value-added
manufacturing?
questions.reply:
A comprehensive national export strategy has
been developed by the Ministry of Commerce in consultation with public and private sector
stakeholders. The strategy aims to enhance Pakistan’s global competitiveness, diversify export
destinations and markets, and strengthen value-added manufacturing. Its overarching framework is
provided through the Strategic Trade Policy Framework (STPF), which offers a long-term,
multi-pronged policy approach comprising the following components:

 Sectoral Roadmaps: Four roadmaps have been developed for the manufacturing and
mining, agriculture, textiles, and services sectors, with tailored policies for each sector
aimed at boosting exports, enhancing value-addition, attracting investment, promoting
sustainability, and developing human capital.
 National Tariff Policy: The Tariff Policy 2025–30 has been introduced, featuring reduced
tariffs on raw materials and intermediary goods, along with the abolition of Additional
Customs Duties (ACDs) and Regulatory Duties (RDs) by 20230. These measures
collectively pass on benefits worth over PKR 120 billion to industry, aimed at lowering
production costs, enhancing competitiveness, and supporting sustainable industrial growth.
 Sectoral Councils: 19 Sectoral Councils headed by private stakeholders, have been
established under STPF 2020-25. The Councils provide policy input to Ministry of
Commerce for growth of their respective sectors.
 Complementary Policies: To create an ecosystem which will promote
manufacturing/industrialization in the country, the following policies provide support to
export enhancement strategies of the Ministry of Commerce:

 Export Finance Scheme (EFS): Designed to provide subsidized short-term financing,
enabling exporters to fulfill orders without facing liquidity constraints.
 New Energy Vehicles Policy 2025–30: Promotes electric and hybrid vehicles with tax
incentives and charging infrastructure to cut emissions and modernize transport.
 Mobile & Electronics Device Manufacturing Policy 2026–33: Drives local
production of phones and electronics, attracting global brands and boosting exports
through strict localization targets.
 Comprehensive Auto & Tractor Policy (Draft): Aims to expand local auto and
tractor manufacturing, integrate with agriculture mechanization, and support export of
auto parts.
 SME Facilitation Initiatives: Launches a digital portal and strengthens SMEDA to
empower small businesses, expand regional trade, and accelerate industrial growth.

This integrated approach is designed to position Pakistan’s exports more competitively in
global markets, while simultaneously building resilience, diversification, and value addition across
sector.

Will the Minister for Federal Education and Professional Training be pleased to state:
a) whether the Ministry intends to declare an " education emergency" and what concrete steps
are planned to address the estimated 25 million out of school children; and
b) how the Ministry will adopt inclusive education models to reduce dropout rates and provide
quality education to underprivileged children?
questions.reply:
(a) The Ministry is treating the issue of out-of-school children as a national priority and is
implementing the following concrete measures:

Enrollment Campaigns:
1. Zero OOSC Enrollment Campaign – ICT (2023): Around 70,000 children enrolled.
2. No Child Left Behind Initiative (2026): Door-to-door surveys in all Union Councils of
Islamabad to identify and enroll approximately 25,000 children.
3. Expansion of Non-Formal Education: Community schools, Accelerated Learning
Programmes (ALPs), second-shift schools, and flexible learning models are being
expanded for children outside the formal system.
4. Retention Measures: Free textbooks, school meal programmes, teacher training, and
community engagement are being implemented to reduce dropouts and sustain
attendance.
5. ICT Plan of Action: Additional classrooms, recruitment of teachers, provision of
missing facilities, evening shifts, home-based education for girls, and digital/hybrid
learning opportunities are being introduced.

(b) The Ministry is adopting inclusive education models through the following targeted
interventions:
1. Establishment of Non-Formal Education Centres, ALPs, community schools, second
shifts, digital/distance learning, and home-based education for girls.
2. Through collaboration with BISP, Zero OOSC Campaign, and No Child Left Behind
Initiative, disadvantaged children are being identified and enrolled.
3. Provision of free textbooks, learning materials, school meal programmes, and improved
school facilities to prevent dropouts.

4. Teacher training, strengthened classroom practices, and community engagement
through Parent-Teacher Councils.
5. Use of EMIS/NEMIS systems, digital monitoring tools, and surveys to identify
excluded children and ensure continued participation.
These measures demonstrate the Ministry’s commitment to equitable access, improved
retention, and quality education for all children, particularly the underprivileged.

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Finance and Revenue be pleased to state:
a) why the 1.21 billion dollars IMF staff-level agreement 1.0 billion dollar EFF, 210 million
dollars RSF was finalized only after talks continued virtually beyond the February, 25 and 2nd
March, 2026 mission;
b) whether this delay reflected unresolved differences on fuel pricing policy now tacitly
endorsed amid the Middle East crisis;
c) whether the Middle East conflict costs a cloud over the outlook with volatile energy prices
risking inflation and growth, yet the Government projects only minor impacts; and
d) what contingency measures exists to meet FY26 primary surplus target of 1.6% of GDP and
FY27 target of 2% if global oil prices remain elevated?
questions.reply:
(a) The
discussions/meetings related to IMF 3rd
Review of Extended Fund Facility (EFF) and 2nd
Review of
Resilience & Sustainability Facility (RSF), were held as per the agreed schedule, i.e., February 25-
March 11, 2026. Meeting with federal and provincial government stakeholders were held in virtual
mode as the visiting IMF Mission Team was directed by the IMF HQs to leave Pakistan in view of the
start of tensions in the Middle East. During February 26-March 11, 2026, the IMF Mission Team
reviewed progress of reforms implemented/being implemented by various government entities as
agreed during the last Review held on September 25-October 08, 2025. Afterwards, the IMF Mission
Team held further meetings with the same quarters to agree on the implementation timelines pertaining
to various structural benchmarks/reforms. Upon conclusion of these two rounds of discussions, the
Memorandum of Economic & Financial Policies (MEFP) was reviewed by the concerned authorities
and was agreed. Accordingly, the Staff-Level Agreement was signed on April 23, 2026.

(b) In continuation of the above, it is further informed that no such delay occurred. The fuel
pricing was adopted by Petroleum Division after detailed deliberation with all the concerned quarters.

(c) The ongoing Middle East conflict, particularly disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, poses an
external risk for Pakistan given its reliance on imported energy. International oil prices have risen
sharply, with Brent crude increasing from $62.7 per barrel in December 2025 to $103.7 in March 2026,
and remaining above $100 amid continued geopolitical uncertainty.
Such oil price shocks transmit through higher import costs, freight charges, and insurance
premiums, creating upward pressure on domestic energy prices and production costs. However,
inflation remains contained, averaging 6.2 percent during Jul-Apr FY2026, well below the 7.5 percent
target for FY2026, and is expected to remain within this target as the government is committed to
mitigating the pass-through of higher global oil prices.
On growth, the near-term impact is expected to be limited due to lagged transmission and
continued economic momentum. GDP growth has remained resilient and provisionally recorded at 3.7
percent in FY2026 against the target of 4.2 percent and contributed by 2.9 percent growth in
agriculture sector, 3.5 percent growth in industrial sector and 4.1 percent growth in services sector.

(d) The primary surplus targets for FY26 and FY27 will be met through a prudent fiscal policy
centered around expenditure rationalization and optimal revenue mobilization. On the expenditure
side, general subsides are being phased-out and replaced with targeted subsidies. Non-essential
expenditures have been curtailed and a comprehensive austerity plan is in place to ensure that
expenditures are kept to bare minimum. The revenue mobilization drive of the Government covers
both policy and enforcement measures. It is also important to note that provincial governments also
contribute towards achievement of primary surplus targets through surpluses.

safe, calm and in the less traffic areas;

Income Tax
Under the provisions of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, essential commodities such as wheat
flour, sugar, edible oil, pulses and other basic foods items are not directly subject to income tax as
goods. Rather, taxation applies to the income of persons engaged in their import, manufacture,
processing, and trading. In this regard:

(i) Agricultural Produce: Income derive from the cultivation of crops such as wheat, rice,
and pulses falls outside the scope of federal income tax in terms of the Constitution and
is subject to provincial taxation.
(ii) Import Stage: Advance tax at the rate of 5.5% of the import value as increased by
customs-duty, sales tax and federal excise duty and 6% of the import value as increased
by customs duty, sales tax and federal excise duty in case of a commercial importer
shall be collected under section 148 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 at the time of
import, by persons importing goods classified in Part-III of the Twelfth Schedule of the

Ordinance. However, reduced rates or exemptions may be notified for essential food
items to avoid undue price impact.
(iii) Supply Chain (Manufacturers/Traders): Individuals and AOP’s receiving payments
on account of supply/sale of rice, cotton seed or edible oils the rate of withholding tax
@ 1.5% shall be applicable under section 153(1)(a) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001.
Withholding tax under section 153 applies to payments for the supply of goods. These
taxes are generally adjustable against their tax liability.
(iv) Minimum Tax Regime : Persons engaged in trading of such commodities may be
subject to minimum tax on turnover under section 113, where applicable.
(v) Final Tax Regimes / Reduced Rates: In certain cases, the Government has prescribed
concessional or final tax regimes for specific sectors dealing with essential commodities
to ease compliance and reduce the effective tax burden.
2. Persons not appearing on the Active Taxpayers List are subject to 100% increased rate of tax
at the import stage as per the Tenth Schedule to the Ordinance.

(b) The Government continues to monitor market conditions and may take appropriate
measures to rationalize the tax burden in order to protect consumers while maintaining fiscal stability.

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Commerce be pleased to state:
a) whether the Government has reviewed Pakistan's Free Trade and Preferential Trade
Agreements to assess their impact on exports, Industrial competitiveness and the trade balance;
if so, the findings thereof;
b) whether it is a fact that several agreements were signed without adequate domestic
industrial capacity, supply-chain readiness, or compliance capability, resulting in import led
growth and weak export performance; if so, the reasons therefor;
c) whether the Government acknowledge that weak alignment between trade concessions and
industrial policy, poor enforcement of rules of origin, and limited utilization of tariff concessions
have undermined the effectiveness of these agreements;
d) whether the Government has evaluated the actual market access obtained under the major
agreements, including China Pakistan Free Trade Agreement (CPFTA), in terms of products
Pakistan can export at scale; and
e) what concrete measures are being adopted to link future trade agreements with industrial
reforms, export competitiveness and measurable performance benchmarks?
questions.reply:
(a) Pakistan has entered into several bilateral
Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) and Preferential Trade Agreements (PTAs) to date. FTAs and PTAs
generally have an in-built clause for review within the agreement and hence periodic review is carried
out with partner countries. The details of these FTAs/PTAs are as under:
i. Malaysia-Pakistan Closer Economic Partnership (MPCEPA): The agreement is
operational since 2008. There is a Joint Review Committee under MPCEPA, which held
its last meeting in May 2025. As agreed by the JRC, MPCEPA is currently
comprehensively being reviewed to ensure its continued relevance and coherence with
evolving trade dynamics and international best practices and to accommodate new and
emerging areas of cooperation such as supply chain resilience, digital trade, SMEs, and
the green economy. The last meeting for review was held on January 26, 2026.
ii. China-Pakistan Free Trade Agreement: After second phase of CPFTA
operationalized in 2020, the difficulties in fully utilizing market access are currently
being discussed with Chinese side. A meeting was held in this regard on February 26,
2026 where concerns of Pakistan were shared with the Chinese side. It may be added
here that China runs a trade surplus with all its trading partners.

iii. Indonesia Pakistan Preferential Trade Agreement: As a result of review of IPPTA,
Indonesia granted unilateral market concession of zero duty to Pakistan on 20 additional
items in 2019. The two sides are currently engaging for further deepening of trade
concessions through negotiation of a CEPA. A meeting was held in this regard on
January 29, 2026.
In case of Indonesia, it may be noted that our major import from Indonesia remains
palm oil, and the trade deficit varies due to its inelastic demand compared to the items
being exported to Indonesia.
iv. PSFTA: Operationalized in 2005, PSFTA has resulted in consistent trade surplus in
favor of Pakistan. The latest meeting to discuss issues under PSTFA was held in
Colombo on 28 January 2026, under the auspices of the Secretary Level Talks (8th
meeting).
v. Uzbekistan Pakistan Preferential Trade Agreement: Uzbekistan Pakistan
Preferential Trade Agreement covers trade in goods. Under the Agreement each country
has given concessions to other on seventeen (17) items. Both sides signed protocol on
5th
Feb 2026, adding 29 additional items in the Preferential Trade Agreement. However,
the Protocol of expansion is not implemented yet.
The volume of bilateral trade between Pakistan and Uzbekistan is increasing
substantially after signing of the Preferential Trade Agreement, with trade surplus in
favour of Pakistan.
vi. Azerbaijan-Pakistan Preferential Trade Agreement: Azerbaijan Pakistan
Preferential Trade Agreement covers trade in goods. Under the Agreement each country
has given concessions to other on nine (9) items.
With the Signing of Azerbaijan and Pakistan Preferential Trade Agreement Pakistan has
surplus trade with Azerbaijan.
vii. Pakistan-Türkiye Trade in Goods Agreement: The Agreement covers trade in goods.
Türkiye has extended concessions to Pakistan on 261 Tariff lines while Pakistan has
extended Turkish side concessions in 130 Tariff Lines. Both sides are negotiating
expansion of the PTA.
Historically, Pakistan has a trade deficit with Turkiye, which remained after signing Trade in
Goods Agreement. Turkiye has imposed stringent non-tariff barriers on import of many
products with export potential from Pakistan, which is one of the reasons behind the
trade deficit.

It may be noted that when a smaller country signs a PTA or FTA with a larger country, the
export of both countries increases. However, the exports of the larger partner increases more as it
generally possess more mature industrial base and economies of scale, producing goods at a lower unit
cost. The impact on exports and trade balance is placed at Annex-A. Impact on Industrial
competitiveness is domain of Ministry of Industries.

(b) No, the agreements were finalized and negotiated/ signed after multiple consultations with
stakeholders in public and private sectors including Ministry of Industries, Engineering Development
Board, Ministry of National Food Security, Ministry of Science and Technology, Federal Board of
Revenue, National Tariff Commission, Chambers of Commerce and Industry, Trade Associations,
Sectoral Councils, importers and exporters of product sectors etc. The tariff concessions are sought and
given with complete input of the relevant industry. To protect our industry, a Sensitive List is prepared
in consultation with all these public and private stakeholders on which no concessions are conceded, to
protect local industry. However, it is important to underscore, that high imports and weak exports
cannot be attributed solely to the provisions of the trade agreement, as a range of internal, external and
structural factors also contribute to the imbalance.

For example, transportation cost and mode is a very important factor in exports. Central Asia,
Iran and Afghanistan have traditionally been very important for exports of Pakistan agricultural
products like rice, meat, kinnow, potatoes, mangoes, sesame seed etc. However, since closure of
borders with Afghanistan, despite PTA/EHP trade has come to a halt. Trade with CARs has declined
drastically despite PTAs, as it was transported through Afghanistan corridor. After Iran-USA War,
Iranian corridor is almost closed as well and sea shipments have become extremely expensive, hurting
exports and disrupting supply chains. Similar situation was faced during covid 19 pandemic. Similarly,
presence of banking channel is extremely important, competitor’s concessions/ agreements are also
important. Domestic factors like cost of energy, stability, exchange rate, policy rate etc. all affect
exports along with external factors.
In order to encourage investment in the country, sometimes such items are included which may
not have a strong industrial base at the moment, but may fetch foreign investment due to concessionary
market access available. Pakistan's objective for liberalization is driven by broader industrial policy
considerations, including attracting foreign investment, facilitating industrial relocation and promoting
value-added exports. The objective is to signal to global investors that Pakistan offers a viable platform
for producing goods destined for the many other markets duty-free.
If Pakistan chooses to wait for "perfect" industrial readiness before signing agreements, it risks
permanent exclusion from global value chains. Pakistan’s competitors are aggressively pursuing Free
Trade Agreements (FTAs) with major hubs. Pakistan cannot compete if its products face a 10-15%
tariff while a competitor’s identical product enters a market duty-free. This results in existing market
share is taken away by competitors who have secured better terms.
Agreements are signed after months and years of negotiations in consultation with relevant
stakeholders as mentioned above. For its part, these trade agreements are in line with the Trade Policy
or Strategic Trade Policy Framework, which is an all-encompassing policy impacting the overall trade
environment of the country. Limited utilization of trade concessions can arise out of multiple factors
such as price competitiveness, NTBs, compliance costs, proximity, cost of transportation, logistics, etc.
Hence it is not correct to attribute effectiveness of trade agreements to above factors only.
(c) Currently, out of over 7500 items at HS 8, Pakistan exports only 50% of them, whereas
imports 80% of them. In FTAs, all items have to be covered, but our utilization capacity is constrained.
In PTAs, existing and potential products are covered, but sometimes, the concessions could not be
utilized. E.g in trade with Azerbaijan, main problem is absence of banking channel, through Iranian
corridor, resultantly taking long route through Poti port of Georgia with long time and high cost of
transportation.
For all of these trade agreements, Certificate of Origin are issued by govt agencies on both
sides and efforts are underway to have them issued and exchanged electronically as well. Enforcement
is by Customs not by Ministry of Commerce, the rules are well enforced and no concessions are given
if importer does not submit COO under the agreement.

(d) Pakistan has different level of market access under its FTAs/PTAs. In general, effort is
made to include all items of export strength in trade agreements. However, the actual market access
availed remains dependent on various factors. Actual market access is often restricted not by tariffs,
but by stringent Sanitary and Phytosanitary (SPS) measures and technical standards. Many local
industries operate at low capacity or face high domestic input costs (energy and credit), preventing
them from achieving the volumes necessary to achieve scale.

(e) The future trade agreements are being negotiated after feasibility studies by 3rd
parties like
FPCCI or PBC etc. with a further stakeholder consultation for the study.
The ongoing negotiations on trade agreements are being conducted after extensive stakeholder
consultations with exporters, industry, associations, chambers of commerce and relevant
government departments to evaluate sector-wise export potential, domestic industrial readiness and
possible impacts on local industry.

Under the Strategic Trade Policy Framework (STPF) 2020-25, market access has been
identified as a key driver of export competitiveness. New trade agreements are being negotiated
carefully to secure market access for value-added products while protecting domestic industry.
Under STPF, a dedicated negotiation cell has been proposed in the Ministry to conduct
objective assessments of trade agreements, strengthen negotiation capacity and ensure better utilization
of concessions through awareness programmes, export diversification initiatives and targeted
engagement in new markets.
National Compliance Centre (NCC) has been established to facilitate compliance with
international standards, bridge global trade laws and help Government to identify sectors where
Pakistan has export potential, assess utilization of tariff concessions, and propose corrective measures
or renegotiations of Trade Agreements, where required.

The curriculum is a living document that is periodically reviewed and updated in light of

NCP. In the study mixed approach qualitative and quantitative was adopted. Findings are as under: -

assignments.
 Teachers lack adequate training for the effective implementation of the NCP
 Insufficient infrastructure and administrative support.

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Federal Education and Professional Training be pleased to state what
strategy is being evolved to identify out-of-school children and ensure their immediate
enrollment in Islamabad in view of the fact that Pakistan has an alarming number of out-of-
school children particularly in Islamabad?
questions.reply:
Under the Prime Minister’s National Education Emergency, the Federal Government has
launched a comprehensive and structured “No Child Left Behind Campaign (2026)” in Islamabad
Capital Territory to ensure complete identification, enrollment, and retention of Out-of-School
Children (OOSC).
This initiative is being implemented through an integrated ICT Action Plan with the following
key components:
Key Measures:
1. No Child Left Behind Initiative (2026) – Core Strategy
 Door-to-door household surveys across all Union Councils of Islamabad.
 Identification, verification, and mapping of Out-of-School Children at household
level.
 Targeted enrollment of approximately 25,000 children into the formal and non-
formal education system.
 Real-time digital tracking of each identified child to ensure follow-up until
admission.

2. Digital Identification & Data Integration
 Geo-tagged household surveys for accurate mapping of OOSC.

 Integration with NFEMIS Portal for real-time registration, monitoring, and
reporting.
 Centralized dashboard for continuous tracking of enrollment progress.

3. Immediate Enrollment Mechanism
 Admission of identified children in nearby public sector schools against available
capacity.
 Operationalization of second shift/evening shift schools where required.
 Establishment and strengthening of Non-Formal Education (NFE) centres.
 Implementation of Accelerated Learning Programs (ALPs) for over-age and out-of-
school children.
4. Retention and Continuity Measures
 Provision of free textbooks and learning materials.
 Attendance monitoring system with dropout alerts and rapid response mechanisms.
 Engagement of parents, communities, and local leaders for sustained enrollment.
 Incentive-based support mechanisms to reduce dropouts.

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Finance and Revenue be pleased to state whether certain dormant accounts
have remained unclaimed by heirs, if so, what is the total amount presently held in said accounts
in each bank at present?
questions.reply:
As per section 31 of
Banking Company Ordinance 1962, a debt payable in Pakistan currency or any other currency owed by
a banking company by reason of a deposit, not being a deposit in the name of a minor or a Government
or a court of law, in respect of which no transaction has taken place and no statement of account has
been requested or acknowledged by the creditor during a period of fifteen years, are considered
unclaimed deposits. Further, all banks/DFIs in Pakistan are required to surrender these unclaimed
deposits to SBP as per the said clause.
Likewise, funds related to all the instruments (e.g. Pay Order, Demand Drafts, Bankers
Cheques, etc.) that have not been paid during the period of 15 years are also required to be surrendered
to SBP. The unpaid funds related to instruments issued in favor of government, are also required to be
surrendered to SBP.
List of accounts surrendered by each bank along with particulars of the account holders is
published on SBP website as well as on the website of the relevant banks. The year wise list of
unclaimed accounts/ funds can be accessed at the SBP website.
The amounts which are surrendered to SBP are allowed to be claimed back by the account
holders / legal heirs. The claimants lodge their claims through their respective banks. The banks, after
scrutiny and due diligence forward the claims to SBP, which are then paid to the claimants.
It may be noted that total amount available with SBP related to Unclaimed Deposits
surrendered by banks as of April 27, 2026 is Rs. 100.59 billion. List of accounts surrendered by each
bank along with particulars of the account holders is published on SBP website as well as on the
website of the relevant banks.

Will the Minister for Finance and Revenue be pleased to state:
a) the obstacles to interest free transactions alongwith the steps being taken to remove the said
obstacles; and
b) the amount of interest that has to be paid for investment and transactions with foreign
countries;
c) whether there is any form of barter system to avoid interest alongwith the detail thereof?
questions.reply:
(a) Islamic banking
in Pakistan has witnessed consistent growth in the last two decades and has emerged as a significant
component of Pakistan’s financial system. As of December 2025, Islamic banking assets represented
23 percent of the overall banking industry, while deposits accounted for a larger portion at 28 percent.
The sector’s share in total financing reached 38 percent, underscoring its growing presence.
Currently, 6 full-fledged Islamic banks along with 15 conventional banks having Islamic banking
branches are offering Islamic financial services in Pakistan. Spread across 146 districts throughout
Pakistan, the branch network of the Islamic banking industry consists of 7,562 branches and 2,932
Islamic windows i.e. dedicated counters at conventional branches.
Furthermore, currently two digital banks are also providing Islamic financial services (one as a
full-fledged Islamic bank while the other through Islamic window operations). These indicators
highlight not only the industry’s sustained progress but also its deeper integration into Pakistan’s
financial architecture. The consistent growth in key Islamic banking indicators and the expanding
branch network demonstrate both the sector’s outreach and the increasing consumer preference in
Pakistan.
Despite witnessing this significant growth there are challenges faced by the Islamic banking
industry that need to be resolved. Accordingly, amongst others, the major obstacles to interest free
transactions include the following:
 Limited availability of Shariah compliant Government securities for liquidity management
of Islamic banking institutions and conversion of existing conventional debt into Islamic
 Shortage of qualified Islamic finance professionals, who can lead the industry into the next
level of growth and development
While SBP has historically been taking several steps to create a conducive and enabling
regulatory environment, SBP along with Government of Pakistan and other stakeholders has
undertaken the major initiatives which are placed at Annex-A.

(b) Quarterly data on interest payments on debt and repatriation of profits/ dividends for the
last one and half years is as below:
The historical data on Pakistan’s external debt and liabilities servicing and income on
investment is available at following links:
1. Pakistan External Debt/Liabilities Servicing https: // www. sbp. org. pk / ecodata /
pakdebtsvr_Arch.xls
2. Repatriation of Profit/ Dividend on Foreign Investment-By Sector https: // www. sbp.
org. pk / ecodata / Repatriation (Archive).xls
Furthermore, Interest payments on External Debt and Repatriation of Profit/ Dividend on
Foreign Investment is at Annex-B.

(c) Barter trade refers to the direct exchange of goods or services without the use of money.
From an Islamic perspective, such transactions are permissible, as they are based on real, asset backed
exchange and avoid Riba (interest). Accordingly, barter arrangements are allowed provided they are
fair, transparent, and free from excessive uncertainty or exploitation. At present, there is no formal or
large-scale barter system operating within Pakistan’s financial or banking sector. Most domestic and

international transactions continue to be conducted through monetary channels supported by the
banking system, ensuring standardization, transparency, and alignment with global financial practices.
However, the Government of Pakistan, through the Ministry of Commerce, has introduced a
limited barter-based trade facilitation mechanism vide SRO 642(I)/2023 dated June 1, 2023, for
Business-to-Business (B2B) transactions with Iran, Afghanistan, and Russia, particularly in cases
where conventional banking channels are constrained due to international sanctions. This framework
has subsequently been refined through SRO 1989(I)/2025 dated October 17, 2025 to address
operational challenges and improve implementation (Annex-C & *Annex-D ).
It is pertinent to note that such barter arrangements operate outside the formal financial system;
hence, the State Bank of Pakistan does not have a direct operational role in these transactions. The
facilitation, regulation, and policy framework for such arrangements fall within the domain of the
Ministry of Commerce, including any bilateral or multilateral trade mechanisms.

(Annexures have been placed in the National Assembly Lirabry)

Will the Minister for Finance and Revenue be pleased to state:
a) why experts warn a sustained oil shock could cost Pakistan 1.5 percent of GDP, with the
external sector facing a Dollar 12-14 billion shock if oil reaches Dollar 120-150 per barrel, yet the
Government maintains only "minor impacts" and has not revised the Dollar 2.2 billion FY 26
current account deficit target;
b) whether petroleum levies contribute over Rs 1,000 billion annually to the budget, yet daily
fuel price adjustments are argued to reduce hoarding and improve fiscal discipline; and
c) what specific mechanism ensures that increased revenue from higher petroleum levies
during price spikes is transparently accounted for and directed toward protecting vulnerable
household rather than lost to inefficiencies?
questions.reply:
(a) Pakistan’s
petroleum imports are around one-fourth of its total import bill. During Jul-Mar FY2026, these
accounted for 22.2 percent. Given the share, the current account is sensitive to changes in oil prices.
However, in first nine months of FY2026, the current account has registered a surplus of $8
million, supported by 8.2 percent growth in workers’ remittances to reach $30.3 billion and IT exports
that increased by 19.8 percent reaching $3.4 billion.
In March 2026, the current account recorded a surplus of $1.1 billion. Despite high volatility in
the oil prices, average Brent crude in March 2026 was recorded at $103.7 per barrels.
The latest external account position remains broadly consistent with the NEC-approved
external sector framework reflected in the Annual Plan 2025-26. The Annual Plan envisages a
contained current account deficit of around $2.1 billion, equivalent to about 0.5 percent of GDP, and
remittances to around US$39.4 billion. In addition, foreign exchange reserve position remains strong.
As of 30th April2026, these were recorded at $21.3 billion. Additional deposits of $3 billion have been
received from Saudi Arabia, along with an extension in terms of the earlier $5 billion deposits and the
government has successfully issued Eurobonds in the international market. IMF EFF program remains
on track. These factors ensure the strengthening of our external buffers to sustain any current account
pressures that may materialize in the future if the conflict in the Middle East prolongs.

Amid a volatile and evolving situation in the Middle East, the downside risks persist. The
impact has remained contained so far, and it is expected to remain within the target range for FY2026.
However, if the shock persists and materially alters the external outlook, projections will be updated
through the normal macroeconomic framework review process during the upcoming APCC and NEC
meetings before the Budget FY2026-27.
The government is closely monitoring the situation and taking timely and proactive measures to
mitigate the impact of these shocks. Under the directives of the Prime Minister, a high- level
committee has been established to monitor daily petroleum supply, secure additional cargoes, and
prevent supply disruptions, along with fuel conservation and austerity measures.

(b) Collection from petroleum levy is dependent on the consumption of petroleum products. In
CFY, an amount Rs. 1,342 billion has been collected for the period July 2025 to April, 2026.

(c) The collection is reported by Petroleum Division, and becomes part of the Federal
Consolidated Fund (FCF) of the Federal Government, wherein all tax and non-tax revenues are
deposited. Expenditure from the FCF is undertaken as approved in the annual budget by the National
Assembly. The approved expenditure in the Budget also includes spending to protect vulnerable
households through various programs, including Benazir Income Support Program, which for FY 2026
is budgeted at Rs. 716 billion.
Furthermore, in the wake of rising fuel prices, the Government has introduced "Energy Relief
Plan" to provide targeted subsidies to vulnerable groups. Under this plan, subsidy is being provided to
motorcycles, public freight and transport, railways and small farmers.

(a)
In the wake of 18th
Constitutional Amendment 2010, the heritage sites along with allied institutions are
devolved to provinces. Heritage sites of Taxila valley are under the Punjab and KPK Archaeology
Departments according to their geographical locations. The conservation work is carried out by Punjab
Archaeology Department as the administrative control of Mohra Muradu and Sirkap archaeological
sites is with them.
However, the Department of Archaeology & Museums (DOAM), Islamabad working under the
administrative control of National Heritage & Culture Division (NH&CD) has communicated with the
Punjab Archaeology Department for exact information about the matter. Punjab Archaeology
Department responded directly to World Heritage Centre in the matter and shared copy with DOAM
(Annex-1).

(b) Permanent Delegate apprised NH&CD about the conservation problems at Taxila sites.
DoAM has communicated the concerns of World Heritage Center and UNESCO about the
conservation of two archaeological sites in Taxila to Punjab Archaeology Department. Punjab
Archaeology Department responded directly to World Heritage Centre in the matter and shared copy
with DOAM (Annex-ll).

(c) DoAM apprised Archaeology Department of Punjab about the concerns of World Heritage
Centre but instead of responding to DOAM, Punjab Archaeology Department has communicated with
World Heritage Center and Permanent Delegate directly and shared copy with DOAM (Annex-Ill).

(d) DoAM has proposed to NH&CD to ask Punjab Archaeology Department to constitute a

In this regard NH&CD had convened a high level meeting (Annex-IV) in the matter in which
all stake holders were invited. The meeting was initially convened on 15th
of April, 2026 then re-
scheduled for 21st
of April, 2026 but could not be held due to work from home orders of Cabinet
Division. Meeting will be held in coming days to sort out the matter.

(e) The DoAM has no information regarding allocation of funds to Taxila as all conservation
work on these sites is being carried out by Punjab Archaeology Department. The information can be

(f) DoAM raised objections of non-inclusion of expert opinion of professional conservator in
the matter of conservation of Mohra Muradu and Sirkap sites. Punjab Archaeology Department has not
responded in the matter as they attached professional opinions of archaeologists in the conservation

Will the Minister for Commerce be pleased to state:
a) whether it is a fact that Pakistan has exported different items of edibles to Middle East
Countries (Kuwait, Qatar, UAE, Oman, Bahrain, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia) during recent Iran,
Israil War;
b) total quantity of all items exported to these countries and total foreign exchange received to
Government; and
c) names of traders/companies who have exported these items?
questions.reply:
(a) Pakistan is exporting various edible items to
Middle Eastern countries including Kuwait, Qatar, UAE, Oman, Bahrain, and the Kingdom of Saudi

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Federal Education and Professional Training be pleased to state the
percentage of the actually spent budget out of allocated education budget during the last Fiscal
Year and the significant progress achieved from the said utilization?

No. 36 was allocated a final budget of Rs. 39.833 Billion, which was fully utilized (100%).

implementation of key education initiatives across ICT, including:

education system.

schools and libraries.

provision of first aid facilities.

for students.

strengthen foundational and skills-based education.

students.

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Commerce be pleased to state:
a) whether it is a fact that appointment at the position of Commercial and Trade Attachés are
also made on contract basis as well from private sector; and
b) details of contract based officers remuneration, qualification, copy of contract?
questions.reply:
(a) The Ministry of Commerce administers
Sixty-Six (66) Pakistan's trade Missions abroad across Fifty-Four (54) countries. These Missions serve
as Pakistan’s principal interface with international trade and investment Partners. Each Mission is
headed by a Trade & Investment Officer (TIO). The selection of the TIOs is carried out through a
transparent and competitive process, strictly in accordance with the Policy Guidelines for the
Selection, Appointment and Posting of TIOs-2024, duly approved by the Honorable Prime Minister.
(Annex-I).
In terms of Para-1(d) of the Policy Guidelines-2024, a minimum of 40%, 50% and 60% of the
vacancies in any particular selection cycle are reserved for BS-20, BS-19 and BS-18 officers of CTG
respectively. Whereas, officers from other Occupational Groups are selected against the remaining
vacancies. Furthermore, in terms of Para 1(f) of the Policy Guidelines-, ibid, 10% quota of TIO’s posts
has been allocated to the candidates from Pakistani Diaspora and Private Sector subject to fulfillment
of prescribed eligibility criteria. In case of non-availability of the suitable candidate against the posts
reserved for CTG and private sector / Pakistan diaspora, the successful public sector candidate from
general pool are appointed against these posts in order of merit.
All candidates from public and private sector are selected through a very competitive and
rigorous selection process. The said selection process involves written test and psychometric
assessment conducted by LUMS / IBA and subsequent interview of the candidates who qualified
written test by a Selection Board chaired by Minister Commerce and having Secretary Commerce,
Secretary MOFA, Secretary SIFC, CE TDAP and an expert from private sector as Members.
It is clarified that only candidates from private sector or Pakistani diaspora are appointed on
contract basis, that too, after they successfully compete and qualify through the transparent and merit-
based selection process. They join their respective posts after security clearance by Special Vetting
Agency (SVA) i.e. Investigation Bureau (IB) and completing pre-departure training at Pakistan
Institute of Trade & development (PITAD).
In the selection cycle (2024-2025), no candidate from the private sector was appointed as no
private sector candidate qualified the written test. However, the list of TIOs appointed from private
sector on contract basis during last Five (05) years is attached as Annex-II.

(b) The qualification requirements for appointment of TIOs from private sector / Diaspora have
been clearly defined in the eligibility criteria prescribed by the Policy Guidelines, 2024.
All officers posted to Pakistan’s Trade Missions abroad are entitled to the same pay packages and
benefits in accordance with the applicable rules and policies. There is no significant difference in
remuneration and perks of the officers appointed from the public sector and private sector.
A copy of the employment contract agreement with the private sector candidate is placed at
(Annex-III).

Minister In-FKDUJHRIWKH3ULPH0LQLVWHU¶V Office: (a) 1. In the disaster management framework
of Pakistan, District Disaster Management Authorities (DDMAs)/ District Administration and Provincial
Disaster Management Authorities (PDMAs) act as the first and second tier responders respectively. NDMA
primarily functions as a coordinating and policy-formulating body. During the monsoon season and other
disaster situations, NDMA regularly issues Daily Situation Reports (SITREPs) based information received
from provinces and relevant stakeholders. These reports provide consolidated updates on losses and
damages as well as response measures, including rescue operations, establishment of relief and medical
camps and relief assistance provided to the affected population.

Monsoon 2025 which caused death toll of 403 human beings and 156 injured.

developed a disaster reporting dashboard. The key features of the dashboard include:-
a. Depiction of number of deaths and injuries.

c. Gender-segregated data.
d. Details of losses (damaged houses, roads, and other infrastructure).
e. Provincial and district-wise breakdown of data.
f. Information on rescue and evacuation operations.
g. Relief assistance provided.
h. Self-explanatory mapping and visualization of disaster impacts.

4. Furthermore, NDMA compiles and publishes post-disaster reports for major national-level events,
such as post-monsoon reports, seasonal reports and incident reports, which provide a comprehensive

assumes the lead role in conducting detailed damage and needs assessments and in formulating recovery
