(a) The Main Line-1 (ML-1) Project is a flagship
initiative of the Ministry of Railways aimed at modernizing Pakistan’s primary railway corridor from Karachi to
Peshawar. The project is being implemented in phases, with the Karachi–Rohri section (approximately 480 km)
currently at an advanced stage of processing in collaboration with the Asian Development Bank (ADB). A Project
Readiness Financing (PRF) loan of US$10 million has been secured, and progress on main loan for Karachi-Rohri
section is in process with ADB. Furthermore, Detailed Engineering Design (DED) and consultant hiring for review
of DED is in progress. Groundbreaking for this section is expected in 2026.
For the remaining sections of ML-1, the Ministry is exploring various financing options and investment
avenues. Overall, the project involves comprehensive upgradation of approximately 1,726 km of track, including
doubling of track from Shahdrah to Peshawar, and selective realignment of about 54 km (Kaluwal–Pindora section)
to improve speed and safety. Key components also include reconstruction of over 2,200 bridges, elimination of 639
level crossings through grade separation, and modernization of the signaling system to international standards.
Once completed, ML-1 will significantly enhance train speeds, improve safety, increase capacity for both
passenger and freight services, and strengthen Pakistan’s overall railway infrastructure.
(b) The Main Line-1 (ML-1) Project has faced delays primarily due to challenges related to financing and
implementation arrangements. Although the project was declared a strategic initiative under the China-Pakistan
Economic Corridor (CPEC) during the 6th Joint Cooperation Committee (JCC) meeting in December 2016, and a
Framework Agreement was signed in 2017, progress remained limited beyond initial preparatory work such as
preliminary design.

The key constraint has been the lack of finalized financing arrangements, despite sustained efforts and
engagement by the Government of Pakistan. As a result, the project could not move into the execution phase.
Subsequently, in consultation with the Chinese side, it was decided to explore alternative financing options through
international partners, including the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and other financial institutions.
Accordingly, the Karachi–Rohri section (approximately 480 km) has been taken up with ADB support,
where preparatory activities are currently underway and implementation is expected to commence shortly. At the
same time, efforts are ongoing to secure financing for the remaining sections of ML-1, including continued
engagement with the Chinese side.
(c) ADB has approved a US$10 million Project Readiness Financing (PRF) loan for the Karachi–Rohri
Section and progress on main loan for Karachi-Rohri section is in process with ADB. Furthermore, remaining
sections of ML-I are open for investment, and several International Financial Institutions (IFIs) are engaged through
Economic Affairs Division (EAD). The Chinese side has also been requested to consider financing the remaining
sections.
(d) The estimated cost and construction period of various sections of the Main Line-I (ML-1) project are as
follows:

i) Karachi–Rohri (480 km): Estimated cost US$ 2.04 billion; groundbreaking expected in 2026.
Construction period is 3 years.
ii) Rohri–Multan (449 km): Estimated cost US$ 1.26 billion; construction period of 3 years.
iii) Multan–Lahore (334 km): Estimated cost US$ 0.88 billion; construction period of 2 years.
iv) Lahore–Rawalpindi (289 km): Estimated cost US$ 1.56 billion; construction period of 3 years.
v) Rawalpindi–Peshawar (174 km): Estimated cost US$ 0.92 billion; construction period of 2 years.

(e) Government has engaged ADB for Financing Karachi - Rohri section of ML-1 and secured ADB Project
Readiness Financing loan of USD 10 million. Detailed Engineering Design of Karachi - Rohri Section is at final
stages. Consultant hiring under PRF loan for review of DED is under process. Furthermore, Government is engaged
with multiple IFIs and Chinese side for financing of remaining sections of ML-1.
(f) The project is being implemented in accordance with international financing procedures, including
competitive procurement, engagement of qualified consultants, phased implementation, and close coordination with
development partners to ensure transparency, efficiency, and timely execution according to International best
practices and standards.

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Water Resources be pleased to state: whether the Government is taking steps to
introduce and expand smart irrigation systems, including drip irrigation and fustigation, in view of increasing
water scarcity and wastage under conventional methods?
questions.reply:
Pakistan is an agrarian economy, with
approximately 95% of its total freshwater withdrawals used by the agriculture sector. At the federal government
level, Indus River System Authority (IRSA) is responsible to distribute available surface water to the provinces as
per Water Apportionment Accord 1991. Irrigation development and adoption of high-efficiency systems such as drip
irrigation and fertigation fall within the provincial domain. The Federal and Provincial governments are
implementing numerous projects on Drip irrigation and fertigation in the country to counter the wastage of water. A
brief of the on-going project in the federal and provinces is following;
Federal Government
Productivity Enhancement through the Installation of Solar-Powered High-Efficiency Irrigation Systems
in ICT (2024 to 2026)
The project is initiated in the ICT area through Ministry of Interior, aiming at improving water use efficiency
of small farming communities within the ICT boundaries. Under the Project, 55 solar pumping systems with High
Efficiency irrigation system (Drip and sprinkler) and Lift irrigation system will be provided to the farmers with a cost
sharing of 80% government and 20% from the farmers share for the better use of water resources in ICT. The total
cost for the project is PKR 529 million. Further details may be obtained from the Ministry of Interior.
Punjab Government
Punjab Resilient and Inclusive Agriculture Transformation (PRIAT) (2022 to 2027)
The project is initiated in all 36 districts of the province, aiming at improving water use efficiency of small-
medium farming communities. Along with other components to improve water use efficiency at field level, Drip
irrigation is the integral component of the project and it is envisaged that High efficiency irrigation systems (Drip and
sprinkler) is planned to be installed on 40,000 acres to reduce water consumption and improve crop yields with a cost
sharing of 75% (Government share) and 25% (farmers share). Further details on the project implementation status
may be obtained from the Punjab Agriculture on Farm Water Management Department.

Transformation of Agriculture in Pothohar (2025-26 to 2027-28)
This project is also initiated by Agriculture Department, Government of Punjab with an objective to bring
uncultivated area under irrigated agriculture through land and water resources development and promotion of high
value agriculture in Pothohar (Attock, Chakwal, Jhelum and Rawalpindi). The project cost is Rs.6,926 million. The
project component includes installation of 1,700 solar coupled lift irrigation schemes, Installation of High Efficiency
Irrigation Systems (HEIS) on 1,700 acres, provision of 270 Laser Land Levelers to the farmers, Construction of 250
watercourses in the command of 15 Small Dams. Further details on the project implementation status may be
obtained from Agriculture Department, Government of Punjab.
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Government
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa irrigated Agriculture Improvement Projects (KP-IAIP), (2019-2026)
This project is being executed in all districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, aiming to improve the performance of
irrigated agriculture for farmers in the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Along with other components, it is envisaged that Drip
and sprinkler irrigation system will be installed at 10,000 acres of land in the province with the subsidy of 60% to the
farmers. The total cost of the project is Rs. 23,943.350 million which is funded by World Bank. Further details may
be obtained from the KP Directorate General of On-Farm Water Management (OFWM).
Sindh Government
Provision of Subsidy assistance on solar power for high efficiency irrigation system (HEIS) (2022-2026)
This project is being executed in all districts of Sindh province. This project is funded by Government of
Sindh. The total cost of the project is Rs. 1204.842 million including GoS Share Rs. 999.286 million and Farmers'
Share Rs. 205.556 million. 353 solar units will be provided to the farmers who have already installed drip irrigation
system under World Bank funded Project Sindh Irrigated Agriculture Productivity Enhancement Project (SIAPEP)
from 2015-2023. These units will be installed on 1725 acres with 80% subsidy to the farmers.
More information on this project may be acquired from the Agriculture Department Sindh.

Will the Minister for Industries and Production be pleased to state:
a) how the Government has finalized National Sugar De-Regulation Policy abolishing the zoning
system and ending price controls in line with IMF commitments will be implemented when Pakistan produces
approximately 6.13 million tonnes of sugar annually from 79 processing mills (seventh largest globally), and
the sector’s value chain is estimated at Rs1.1 trillion;
b) whether the policy introduces third-party weighing systems, improved credit access, and
mechanization support for farmers, with full liberalization targeted from November, 2026 yet critics warn
removing controls without breaking the concentration of power among politically connected mill owners (as
documented in SECP shareholding reports) could allow the sugar cartel to set prices more freely, leading to
higher consumer costs while small farmers remain vulnerable to delayed payments; and
c) what competition oversight mechanism exists to prevent monopolistic behavior post-deregulation?

Minister for Industries and Production: (a) The Prime Minister constituted a Committee to firm up
proposals for deregulating Pakistan’s sugar sector under the chairmanship of Minister for Power on 17th
July, 2025.
Ministry of Industries and Production provided Secretarial support to the committee. The draft De-Regulation Policy
has been formulated after holding series of meetings with the Provincial Governments, growers’ association and
Pakistan Sugar Mills Association. Therefore, the draft recommendations shared with the provinces. Three (3)
provinces agreed and one province i.e., Government of Sindh shared its reservations to some of the proposed
deregulation measures which are under consideration process right now. It is pertinent to mention that it is the
structural benchmark of IMF according to which the policy will be approved by the end June, 2026.
(b) To ensure a smooth transition, the draft deregulation policy provides targeted supporting measures. By
these measures, growers’ interest will be protected by mandating third-party verification of cane weighing, statutory
interest on delayed payments, improved access to credit, mechanization programs, and industry-funded research and
development. Market stability will be created through the establishment of a one-month rotating sugar buffer stock,
stronger quality enforcement and improved market information systems. In last two crop years, the Provincial
Governments deregulated sugarcane indicative prices. Consequently, the growers got better prices. The comparative
study of deregulation of other crops like rice also indicates that deregulation resulted in more production, more
exportable surplus, introduction of advance varieties and better farmer economics. Countries that moved from tightly
controlled regimes to more market-oriented systems offer practical, context-sensitive lessons on the sequencing,
safeguards, and complementary policies. In the context of this policy, the case of Brazil and Thailand is important.
The draft deregulation policy proposes that competition and oversight will be strengthened through enhanced
capacity of the Competition Commission to prevent collusion and market abuse.
(c) Moreover, the recommendations of the Committee free entry of new entrants in the business while
removing all restrictions. Due to free market mechanism the monopoly of some players is not possible. Moreover, by
strengthening Competition Commission of Pakistan, all kind of malpractices can be curbed by taking appropriate
action against the culprits.

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Water Resources be pleased to state whether any study has been undertaken
during the last three years to assess groundwater resources in Islamabad Capital Territory; if so, the details
and key findings thereof?
questions.reply:
Management of Groundwater
resources in Islamabad falls under Ministry of Interior’s mandate through the Capital Development Authority (CDA),
Islamabad; however, Ministry of Water Resources through its affiliated department i.e. Pakistan Council of Research
in Water Resources (PCRWR) has undertaken Groundwater assessment in the Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT)
during 2022-23, (Annexure-I). The study provides assessment of groundwater resource in terms of depth to water
table variations, resource availability, recharge sources, water quality status and spatial mapping. The key findings
are as follows:
 The depth to water table (DTW) varies spatially and ranges from 15 m to more than 100 m. The
average DTW lies in the range of 35 – 40 m. It is analyzed that DTW is generally deeper in the areas
where, dependence on groundwater is higher compared to surrounding areas.
 The areas such as Sectors G-11,13,14,15,16, F-11, Ghori town, Gangal East, Jinnah Garden and Navel
Anchorage have relatively deeper groundwater table ranging 60 – 106 m.
 The urbanization reduces the groundwater recharge and excessive groundwater abstraction disrupts the
natural balance, leading to water table depletion at an estimated rate of about 1 m per year in
Islamabad..
 The availability of groundwater potential evaluated up to 300 m depth of aquifer indicated that
maximum potential is concentrated at a depth of 150 m, covering approximately 63% of the area
within the moderate to good potential zone. Overall active storage of groundwater potential covering
moderate and good potential zones is 7.5 BCM.
 The natural groundwater recharge potential is high near the Margalla hills whereas, it gradually
decreases while moving towards Faizabad area. Rainfall is the major source of recharge in the area
with minor contribution from surface sources i.e. streams.
The most prevailing contaminants were found to be bacteriological contamination, hardness, nitrate and
turbidity. The primary cause of microbiological contamination is the untreated disposal of waste water in fresh water
streams, which ultimately pollute both surface water bodies and groundwater resource.

(Annexure has been placed in the National Assembly Library)

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Railways be pleased to state:
a) whether the Government has conducted a nationwide assessment of the condition of Railways tracks,
bridges, signaling systems, and other critical infrastructure; and
b) the details of funds allocated in the current Financial Year for repair, rehabilitation, and upgrading of
Railways infrastructure?
questions.reply:
(a) Pakistan Railways has conducted
comprehensive and continuous assessments of railway tracks, bridges, signaling systems, and other critical
infrastructure across the entire network.
All railway bridges are subjected to detailed inspections on a semi-annual and annual basis to accurately
assess their structural condition and ensure safety.
With regard to railway tracks, Pakistan Railways has undertaken a system-wide survey and assessment
covering its entire network of approximately 11,881 track kilometers and 7,791 route kilometers. These assessments
have revealed that a significant portion of the track infrastructure has exceeded its useful life, with varying degrees of
over-aged track across Main Lines and branch lines. In order to ensure passenger safety, Engineering Speed
Restrictions have been imposed on vulnerable sections. A well-defined multi-tier inspection and monitoring
mechanism is in place under the Way and Works Manual, involving field officers at divisional levels, along with the
issuance of Annual Safety Certificates confirming the fitness of tracks for train operations. Routine maintenance is
carried out through revenue funding, while rehabilitation and upgradation works are undertaken through PSDP
projects and other development initiatives.
Regarding signaling systems, Pakistan Railways maintains a diverse mix of technologies, including
mechanical, relay-based and computer-based systems, many of which are obsolete. The condition of signaling
infrastructure is regularly assessed through inspections, audits, and field evaluations. These assessments have
identified the need for phased modernization and rehabilitation. Accordingly, multiple projects are being
implemented, including the installation of Computer-Based Interlocking (CBI) systems, communication system
improvements, replacement of obsolete equipment and infrastructure rehabilitation under various development
programs.
Overall, these assessments are part of an ongoing and structured mechanism to monitor infrastructure
condition, ensure operational safety, and plan timely rehabilitation and modernization of Pakistan Railways’ critical
assets.
(b) During the current financial year 2025-26, funds have been allocated under the heads “Revenue,”
“Improvement Fund and Welfare Expenditure,” and “PSDP” for the repair, rehabilitation, and upgradation of railway
infrastructure. An amount of approximately Rs. 2,600 million has been allocated under Head Revenue, Rs. 421
million under Improvement Fund and Welfare Expenditure, and Rs. 2,274 million under PSDP have been allocated.
Details are attached at Annexure A.

(Annexure has been placed in the National Assembly Library)

questions.ministry: National Health Services, Regulations and Coordination
questions.question:
Will the Minister for National Health Services, Regulation and Coordination be pleased to state:
a) what national policy framework has the Government devised for population planning;
b) how is effective coordination with the provinces is being maintained, particularly in light of the
Eighteenth Amendment to the Constitution of Pakistan; and
c) whether the Federal Government collaborating with and providing support io NGOs and
INGOs engaged in population planning to ensure a unified and cohesive national strategy?
questions.reply:
(a)
1. CCI Recommendations on population: The recommendations approved by the Council of Common
Interests (CCI) (2018) have been adopted as National Strategic Framework on population planning at
national and sub-national levels. The CCI Recommendations are focused on eight (08) thematic areas
to achieve the target of population stabilization in the country.

2. National Action Plan on Population (2019-2024): For the operationalization of the CCI
Recommendations, the Ministry of National Health Services, Regulations & Coordination (M/o
NHSR&C), in consultation with the provincial & regional governments and other stakeholders,
developed a National Action Plan on Population (2019-2024).
3. Revised National Action Plan on Population (2025-2030): M/o NHSR&C, in consultation with the
provinces, regions and other stakeholders, has revised the NAP with timeline of 2025-30, keeping in
view the high population growth as revealed in census 2023 and recommendations of the Supreme
Court Conference on Population (2023).
4. National Narrative on Population: The narrative has been adopted at national and sub-national levels.
It empowers parents to have the right to freely and responsibly decide the number and spacing of their
children to fulfil the fundamental rights of their children and family by maintaining a
Balance/Tawazun between their family size and resources.
5. The Draft National Health and Population Policy (202635) which is in process of approval, represents
the successor to the National Health Vision (2016-25). Drafted by the Ministry of National Health
Services, Regulations & Coordination, this policy serves as a strategic "compass" to integrate health
and population management into a single, cohesive framework.
(b) Coordination with provinces is ensured through different federal-provincial forums:
1. Federal Task Force (FTF) on Population: It is the highest-level steering and oversight body chaired by
president of Pakistan to ensure that the recommendations approved by the Council of Common
Interests (CCI) are translated into action across both federal and provincial levels.
2. Inter-Ministerial Health and Population Council: It a coordination body within the Ministry of
National Health Services, Regulations & Coordination (NHSRC) which acts as the technical and
operational bridge between federal and provincial ministries to ensure health and population reforms
are implemented uniformly.
3. Country Engagement Working Group (CEWG): This Technical Group meets quarterly to review
progress, address implementation challenges, and harmonize population interventions across
provinces. Its members include Secretaries of provincial and regional population and health
departments.
(c) The Government engages with NGOs/INGOs to ensure coherent and coordinated population planning
efforts. The collaboration includes:
 CSOs are members of the Country Engagement Working Group
 CSOs Focal Point is member of FTF
 In preparing National Action Plans on population and National Narrative on population, NGOs/INGOs
were consulted in detail.
 Technical guidance and alignment with national population strategies.
 Capacity-building programs for service providers.
 Support for service delivery and awareness campaigns, particularly in underserved areas.

(a) Pakistan Railways procure goods and
services including electrical and mechanical spares for rolling stock, signaling spares and civil contracts
annually in accordance with PPRA rules.
Following procurement units are established in Pakistan Railways
 Headquarters Office, Lahore under Chief Controller of Purchase.
 Procurement Directorate, Islamabad under Director Procurement.
A proper mechanism to ensure quality and timelines is in place and for quality check the items are initially
inspected by District Controller of Purchase/Inspection as per specification given in the contracts.

Further, third-party inspection mechanism through pre-qualifications of 5 firms has also been put in place to
strengthen the transparent inspection of material through an independent firm.
In case of any discrepancy, the material is rejected and processed for replacement. Furthermore, satisfactory
warranty period is ensured through performance bond as per guidelines of PPRA Rules Clause 39.
However, if any deviation in quality or timeline is observed on the part of contractor then contractors are
penalised either through LD or termination of contract or black listing.
Due to non fulfilment of contractual provisions, ten firms have been blacklisted.
(b) The details of said cases are attached as (Annex-A ) clearly mentioning the action taken, against the
defaulting firm.

questions.ministry: National Health Services, Regulations and Coordination
questions.question:
Will the Minister for National Health Services, Regulations and Coordination be pleased to state:
a) whether it is a fact that the Ministry has sought legal opinions on various matters relating to the Pakistan
Nursing and Midwifery Council from the Ministry of Law and Justice, Establishment Division, and other
regulatory forums during the last three years, particularly on the recommendations of constitutional
institutions, including Parliamentary Committees; if so, the details thereof;
b) what corrective actions were proposed or required to be taken by the Ministry in light of such legal
opinion;
c) whether the said corrective measures have been implemented; if so, the details thereof; if not, the reasons
thereof; and
d) the steps being taken to ensure compliance and institutional accountability in lights of above?
questions.reply:
(a) Various legal opinions/advice have been sought by the Ministry of National Health Services, Regulations
and Coordination on different matters relating to the Pakistan Nursing and Midwifery Council, as and when required,
from the Ministry of Law and Justice, Establishment Division, and other relevant forums during the last three years.
It is further submitted that the Pakistan Nursing and Midwifery Council Ordinance is presently in force.
Consequently, matters relating to the Council, including its administrative and regulatory functioning, are being dealt
with under the said Ordinance. Furthermore, all employees of the Council shall be governed by the new service
regulations to be framed/notified under the existing legal framework.
(b) The corrective measures proposed/required to be taken included strengthening the legal and regulatory
framework of the Pakistan Nursing and Midwifery Council, framing of new rules/regulations, streamlining of
administrative and regulatory functions, and initiation of action in cases where appointments or other actions were
found to have been made contrary to law. Accordingly, the Pakistan Nursing and Midwifery Council Ordinance,
2025 has been promulgated and is presently in force. The Ordinance provides a strengthened legal framework for
regulation, administration, inspection, accreditation, registration, licensing, and institutional accountability of the
Council.
(c) The disciplinary actions have been initiated and are under progress. Under the PNMC Act,
rules/regulations shall be framed thereunder to replace the weak regulatory framework in the past to ensure
transparent, lawful, and merit-based functioning of the Council. It is assured that where any appointments or other
actions were found to have been made in violation of law, inquiry proceedings shall be initiated.
(d) The Pakistan Nursing and Midwifery Council Ordinance, 2025 provides a strengthened mechanism to
ensure compliance and institutional accountability as under:
1) Under section 38 of the Ordinance, the Division concerned may, on receipt of information or
complaint or on its own motion, constitute a Commission of Inquiry headed by an officer not
below BS-20 along with a subject expert.
2) The Commission has powers equivalent to a Civil Court for summoning persons, enforcing
attendance, examining persons on oath, compelling production of documents including
digital evidence, receiving evidence on affidavits, and issuing commission for examination
of witnesses.

3) The Commission is required to fix responsibility within ninety days and submit its report to
the Secretary of the Division concerned for appropriate action.
4) Further, section 20 of the PNMC Ordinance, 2025, provides a review/appellate mechanism
whereby any aggrieved person or institution may seek review of a decision of the Council
regarding nursing institutions before the Secretary of the Division concerned within thirty
days.
5) The Ordinance provides for annual reporting, furnishing of
reports/returns/statistics/documents to the Division concerned, public dissemination of real-
time data, SOPs, guidelines and reports on the Council’s website, and binding policy
directives of the Federal Government.

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Railways be pleased to state: whether Pakistan Railways is undertaking any
modernization or digitization projects in collaboration with China or involving the private sector; if so, the
details thereof?
questions.reply:
Yes, Pakistan Railways is actively undertaking
modernization and digitization on public private partnership mode involving both international partners including
China and the private sector. The key projects in this regard are as follows:
RABTA (Railway Automated Booking and Travel Assistance) Platform:
Pakistan Railways has implemented a passenger facilitation and e-ticketing system, namely RABTA, which has been
awarded to M/s Easyway JV Norinco under a Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) model. This project represents a
collaboration involving the private sector as well as an international partner. Under this arrangement, the consortium
is responsible for the development, operation, and maintenance of the system for a specified concession period, after
which it will be transferred to Pakistan Railways. RABTA provides end-to-end digital services including online
ticketing, mobile application interface, payment gateway integration, and real-time passenger facilitation,
significantly enhancing service delivery and revenue generation. The statistical data pertaining to RABTA project
and the digitization footprints under this initiatives are given below in image, pasted below:

I. RAIN (Railway Advanced Infrastructure Network):
Pakistan Railways has also launched its flagship digitization initiative, the Railway Advanced Infrastructure
Network (RAIN), which is being implemented under a Government-to-Government (G2G) arrangement with
the Frontier Works Organization (FWO), through its subsidiary, ONE NETWORK—an entity with a proven
track record in the modernization and full digitization of Pakistan’s motorway infrastructure.
The RAIN project is aimed at establishing a robust and integrated digital backbone for Pakistan Railways. Its scope
includes the deployment of optical fiber connectivity along approximately 1,700 kilometers of the ML-1
corridor; GPS-based train tracking systems; RFID-enabled asset monitoring covering passenger coaches,
locomotives, and freight wagons; centralized Rail-Tag-based Weigh-in-Motion (WIM) systems; and the
development of Safe and Smart Railway Stations through AI-enabled surveillance to enhance passenger
safety. Additionally, the project incorporates real-time fuel monitoring and the establishment of centralized
command and control centers, extending from Headquarters to all seven divisional offices, ensuring end-to-
end visibility of train operations. Furthermore, onboard train surveillance systems are being deployed on an
initial set of four trains under Phase-I, funded through Pakistan Railways’ own revenue.

RAIN is designed to enable real-time operational monitoring, improve efficiency, strengthen safety
mechanisms, and facilitate data-driven decision-making across the entire railway network.
Infrastructure Modernization/Up-gradation Projects
I. Mainline – 1 (ML-1)
Mainline – 1 (ML-1) is the backbone of Pakistan Railway network catering to the bulk of its passenger and
freight transportation. Upgradation of ML-1 is a strategic project under CPEC and significant milestones
have been achieved in collaboration with China like the feasibility and preliminary design. Pakistan is
actively pursuing financing options for upgradation of various sections of ML-1. In this regard, Pakistan
Railways is enagaged with ADB for upgrwadation of Karachi-Rohri section of ML-1 (480km). Groundwork
is underway and the groundbreaking of the project is expected later this year. Furthermore, Pakistan side has
requested the Chinese side to consider financing remaining sections of ML-1 (Rohri-Peshawar).
II. Dedicated Freight Corridor (DFC)
The Dedicated Freight Corridor (DFC) project is an important initiative to shift containerized cargo from
road to rail and improve freight movement in Karachi. It involves development of a 50 km dual-track rail
corridor from Karachi Port to Pipri Marshalling Yard, along with rolling stock and a Multi-Modal Logistics
Park (MMLP). The project is being implemented in phases: Phase-I comprises a pilot investment of USD 20
million, Phase-II will include full construction of the dedicated dual-track corridor and expansion of logistics
infrastructure to achieve complete operationalization of the DFC.
Currently, Phase-I is under implementation, with ground-breaking 0n 09,01.26. Upon completion, the DFC
project is expected to reduce road congestion, improve safety, improve port efficiency, lower environmental impact,
and enhance the overall competitiveness of Pakistan’s logistics and trade sector through faster and more reliable
freight movement.

questions.ministry: National Health Services, Regulations and Coordination
questions.question:
Will the Minister for National Health Services, Regulations and Coordination be pleased to
state:
a) whether it is a fact that the main energy drinks contain from about 50 to 500 milligrams of
caffeine per serving;
b) whether it is also a fact that increased caffeine levels consumed by children can cause a
wide range of health consequences some of these adverse effects are serious enough to require
seeking medical help; and
c) if so, what steps are being taken by the Ministry?
questions.reply:
(a) Yes, the caffeine content in energy drinks varies depending on the brand and serving size.
International evidence indicates that most of the energy drinks contain approximately 50 mg to over 300
mg of caffeine per serving, while some larger containers or highly concentrated products may contain up
to 400-500 mg per container, (source: American Academy of Pediatrics)
In Pakistan, energy drinks available in the market fall within similar ranges; however, caffeine
content may vary, and labeling compliance is regulated under national food safety frameworks.

(b) Yes, this is also a well-established fact. According to the World Health Organization,
excessive caffeine intake in children and adolescents can result in:
 Increased heart rate and elevated blood pressure
 Anxiety, irritability, and sleep disturbances
 Gastrointestinal disturbances
 In severe cases, caffeine toxicity requiring medical attention

(c) In Pakistan, there is no single dedicated federal law exclusively regulating energy drinks;
however, the matter is governed through a combination of food safety laws, standards, and provincial
regulatory actions/ The energy drinks do not come under the regulatory ambit of the Ministry of National
Health Services, Regulations and Coordination (NHSR&C), however, in coordination with provincial
authorities, the Government has undertaken the following measures:
Regulatory Oversight:
Coordination with Pakistan Standards and Quality Control Authority and provincial food authorities
(e.g., Punjab Food Authority) to ensure compliance with labeling requirements, including disclosure of
caffeine content and health warnings.
1. Restrictions for Children:
Provincial food authorities have issued advisories discouraging the sale and marketing of
energy drinks to children, and monitoring compliance in educational institutions.
2. Public Awareness Campaigns:
Occasionally, Awareness initiatives are being conducted to educate the public, particularly
parents and youth, regarding the health risks of excessive caffeine consumption.

3. Integration in NCD Prevention:

The issue of unhealthy dietary practices, including high caffeine intake, is being addressed
under broader National Action Framework for Non-Communicable Diseases (NCD)
prevention and Mental Health (2021-2030)

Energy drinks contain varying but often high levels of caffeine, and excessive intake particularly
among children poses significant health risks. The Government of Pakistan is addressing this issue through
regulatory measures, awareness campaigns, and integration into national health strategies to protect public
health.

Will the Minister for Housing and Works be pleased to state:
a) the policy devised to vacate the houses constructed in Sector G-12 Islamabad;
b) the rate of build-up property given to the owners of the vacated houses;
c) whether it is a fact that despite the enforcement of Section 144 against construction in
Sector G-12 Islamabad, shops and houses are being constructed rapidly; if so, why the construction is
not being stopped;
d) whether it is also a fact that an operation was conducted to clear the service roads of Sector
G-12 and G-13 Islamabad, houses were demolished, and since then, shops, hotels, and showrooms are
being reconstructed there;
e) if so, why their reconstruction is not being stopped; and
f) the time by which Sector G-12 Islamabad will be vacated?

Minister for Housing and Works (Mian Riaz Hussain Pirzada) (a) The policy for vacating
houses constructed in Sector G-12, Islamabad has been formulated in accordance with applicable laws
and the mandate of FGE Housing Authority. Under this policy, notices are issued to occupants of
encroached or illegally constructed structures, affording them an opportunity to vacate voluntarily within a
specified timeframe. In cases of non-compliance, enforcement actions are undertaken through anti-
encroachment operations in coordination with the local administration and law enforcement agencies.
However, the sector can only be fully vacated upon formal announcement of the BUP awards.
(b) The award of BUPs in Sector G-12, Islamabad is yet to be announced. As the sector
constitutes a new allocation, specific compensation rates are required to be determined and applied
accordingly. The valuation is undertaken on a case-to-case basis, taking into account the nature of the
structure and the prevailing notified rates/assessed values. These rates are subject to formal approval by
the Executive Board of FGE Housing Authority, which is currently pending.
(c) At present, Section 144 Cr. P.C. is not in force in Sector G-12, Islamabad. However,
sporadic instances of construction activity have been observed despite the fact that
compensation to landowners is still pending.
 It is a well-settled legal principle that upon issuance of an Award and the subsequent vesting
of acquired land in the Federal Government or the acquiring entity under the Land Acquisition
Act, 1894, the rights of affected persons are confined solely to the receipt of compensation. No
individual is legally entitled to erect new structures, expand existing ones, or occupy the
acquired land under any pretext, as both title and possession vest irrevocably in the acquiring
authority.
 During the period when Section 144 was imposed by the Islamabad Capital Territory
Administration, both major and minor anti-encroachment operations were conducted, resulting
in the demolition of multiple unauthorized structures, and six (06) FIRs were registered against
encroachers.
 There is no significant surge in illegal construction within the sector; however, whenever any
unauthorized activity is reported by the Enforcement and Vigilance Directorate, FGE Housing
Authority takes prompt action to demolish such structures. In the meantime, compensation to
landowners remains pending.
 Furthermore, several communications have been made with the district administration ICT for
conducting a comprehensive anti-encroachment operation. However, owing to the prevailing
law and order situation, the ICT administration has expressed its inability to re-impose Section
144 Cr. P.C. in FGEHA-acquired sectors, particularly Sector G-12.
 Meanwhile, notices have been issued to the individuals involved in illegal construction.
(d) & (e)

 Compensation to landowners is still pending. Furthermore, in light of the judgment of the
Islamabad High Court, the Enforcement and Vigilance Wing of FGE Housing Authority is
authorized only to issue notices, which have already been duly served.
 It is emphatically stated that once land is acquired and vested in the acquiring entity, no
person—whether a former landowner, affectee, or any other occupant—has any legal right to
raise new structures or reconstruct demolished ones on such land. Accordingly, whenever
instances of reconstruction occur, particularly along the service roads of Sectors G-12 and G-
13, such structures are removed through enforcement operations carried out by the
Enforcement and Vigilance Wing.
 Action against encroachments is to be undertaken by the Islamabad Capital Territory Police,
while the DC/LAC coordinates with ICT Police for this purpose. However, the Enforcement and
Vigilance Wing continues to face challenges due to resistance from encroachers and repeated
violations.
(f) No definitive timeline can be specified at this stage for the complete vacation of
Sector G-12, Islamabad. The vacation process is contingent upon the formal announcement of
the BUP awards. However, FGE Housing Authority is actively pursuing necessary measures to
expedite the clearance of the sector.

(a) Pakistan Railways has operated at a

result, Pakistan Railways recorded a marked turnaround from an operating loss of Rs. 8.460 billion in FY
2022-23 to an operating surplus of Rs. 0.412 billion in FY 2023- 24, further improving to an operating
surplus of Rs. 2.417 billion in FY 2024-25. Detail of Operating Performance for the last 5 years is given

Over the past decade (2012–2025), the organization has consistently incurred significant losses,
primarily due to heavy expenditures on salaries, pensions, high-speed diesel (HSD) oil, and utilities. The
following financial data from 2020-21 to 2024–25 reflects persistent annual deficits ranging from
approximately Rs. 47 billion to Rs. 60 billion. These recurring losses are bridged each year through Grant-
in-Aid provided by the Federal Government, without which Pakistan Railways would face severe financial
shortfalls.
Over the last 15 years, no loans or financial assistance have been sought from any financial
organization or international institution.
Pakistan Railways strategy is to combine modernizing assets, privatizing parts of operations,
improving efficiency, recovering railway land, and upgrading infrastructure to transform Pakistan Railways
into a more profitable and sustainable organization.
The following key steps taken by the Pakistan Railways to eliminate the losses of Pakistan Railways
and improve its financial and operational situation.

1. Modernization and Fleet Renewal.
 Procurement of up to 275 new locomotives and rehabilitation of old locomotives through various
funding sources to improve efficiency and reduce breakdown-related losses.
 Induction of high-speed coaches (160 km/h), with 46 coaches already delivered, to improve
passenger services and increase revenue.
 Procurement of 820 high-capacity freight wagons of international standards; raw material for 230

wagons has been received.
 Induction of high-capacity/high-speed hopper bogies for efficient coal transportation and un
loading.
2. Public-Private Partnerships (PPP) and Outsourcing.
 Private sector involvement in rehabilitation of locomotives, development of dry ports, and
commercial management of passenger trains.
 Four passenger trains have been outsourced, with plans to outsource 11 more, expected to generate
Rs. 8.5 billion in additional revenue.
 Outsourcing of non-core services such as railway schools and hospitals to reduce financial burden.
3. Opening Infrastructure to Private Operators
 Introduction of the Track Access Regime, allowing private operators to run freight trains on
Pakistan Railways’ infrastructure by paying track access charges.
 This initiative helps utilize idle capacity and generate additional revenue without public investment.
4. Cost-Cutting Measures
 Workforce rationalization under IMF-linked reforms, including a reduction of approximately 18%
of surplus staff.
 Contract with Pakistan State Oil (PSO) for optimal fuel utilization, expected to save 8–10% of the
fuel bill.
 Handing over residential colonies to DISCOs/K-Electric for direct electricity billing, saving an
estimated Rs. 1.8 billion annually.
 Installation of solar power systems in office buildings to reduce utility expenses.
5. Land and Asset Management
 Government-led operations to recover encroached railway land, which can be monetized or used for
commercial purposes.
 Improved asset utilization to generate recurring revenue streams.
6. Infrastructure Upgrades
 Investment in track rehabilitation, modern signaling systems, and safety improvements to reduce
delays, accidents, and maintenance costs.
 Long-term projects such as Main Line-1 (ML-1) and upgrades on key routes (e.g., Rohri–Karachi,
Lahore–Rawalpindi) to enhance speed, capacity, and reliability.
7. Revenue-Generating Initiatives
 Launch of premium services such as Pak Business Express.
 Rationalization of fares along with improved services.
 Stronger enforcement against fare evasion.
 Resumption of the Islamabad–Tehran–Istanbul (ITI) Cargo Train on 21-12-2021 after nine years,
enhancing regional connectivity and freight revenue.
8. Technological Interventions
 Implementation of SAP ERP system for real-time costing, financial control, and informed decision-
making.
 Replacement of outdated systems with modern technology to improve operational efficiency.
9. Customer Facilitation Services
 Introduction of RAABTA, an integrated digital platform enabling trip planning, seat selection,
ticket purchase, train tracking, meals, car rentals, and hotel bookings.
 Expansion of online e-ticketing through JazzCash, UBL Omni, and credit cards to attract more
passengers and improve transparency.
10. Privatization of Subsidiaries
 Privatization of RAILCOP, PRFTC, PRACS, and REDAMCO under the SOEs Act, 2023, aimed at
improving efficiency and reducing the financial burden on Pakistan Railways.

SAEED AHMAD MAITLA
Acting Secretary

2
electricity consumers. Further, the ‘Prime Minister Efficient Fan Replacement Program’ is underway

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Energy (Petroleum Division) be pleased to state:
a) the steps being taken by the Government in near future for the provision of
inexpensive Gas/RLNG to the public; and
b) whether Government is making any plan in this regard?
questions.reply:
(a) Expensive RLNG is
diverted to domestic sectors at notified indigenous gas tariff which results into tariff differential or
diversion cost. This cost is recovered from all other consumers of gas through cross subsidy
mechanism. The domestic sector is bifurcated into protected and non-protected categories based on
minimum consumption threshold. 67% of the domestic consumers fall in protected category which are
charged Rs. 200 to 350 per mmbtu as against average purchase price of Rs. 1,800 per million BTUs.
So the domestic sector is already getting subsidies gas and RLNG. Rest of the consumers other than
domestic sector are unable to carry the burden of cross subsidy as the same is not budgeted like tariff
differential subsidy in power sector. Under the reforms agenda, Government plans to replace the cross-

7

subsidy with direct financial support for low-income households through a social support program like
BISP. Previously, domestic consumers were provided gas at subsidized rates regardless of their income
level, and the subsidy structure was largely consumption-based. This subsidy was effectively financed
through higher tariffs charged to industrial and commercial consumers, which placed an additional cost
burden on productive sectors of the economy. The new approach aims to link subsidies with income
levels by utilizing existing social protection mechanisms such as the Benazir lncome Support
Programme (BISP). Through this system, only eligible and low-income households will receive
subsidy on gas usage while there will be full cost recovery so that circular debt in the gas sector is
avoided.

(b) Same as above.

Will the Minister for Science and Technology be pleased to state:
a) the modus operandi of Fairness Creams, registration, license, quality and how to
ensure human safety;

b) whether Ministry is aware of the presence of hazardous substances such as
mercury among other in fairness creams;

c) whether any study or testing has been conducted to assess the safety and long term
health effects; and

years?
questions.reply:
(a) Federal Government
under section 14 of PSQCA Act VI of 996 has prohibited the manufacturing, keeping in stock and sale
of skin cream that do not conform to the relevant standard specification vide SRO. NO. 45(KE)2017,
02- 05/2017. (Attached as Annexure-A). PSQCA has developed Pakistan Standard specification 3228-
2025 for skin cream harmonized with international standards and safety guidelines. Limits of
hazardous elements like mercury, arsenic, hydroquinone, corticosteroid, microbiological parameters
are addressed in the standard in line with international standards and requirements. PSS 3228-2025
“Pakistan Standard for Cosmetics” Skin Cream is attached as Annexure-B. PSQCA licenses are issued
to manufacturers of skin creams as per procedures laid down in Pakistan Conformity Assessment
(PCA) Rules 2011 that include inspection visit of the manufacturing site and testing of the product in
accordance with standard specifications in order to ascertain quality of the product. PCA Rules, 2011
attached as Annexure -C.

substances, including mercury, in certain Cosmetic products such as Skin fairness creams. In response,

These standards have been made legally binding under the applicable regulatory framework
and are enforced through mandatory testing, quality control mechanisms, and routine market
surveillance. The PSS 3228-2025 have been made mandatory for compliance by PSQCA. Continuous

circulation of unsafe cosmetic products in market.

Reports from PCSIR showed that the following brands were found non-conforming to PSS

(a) National Highways and
Motorway Police (NHMP), following international standards for accident reporting, prepare a detailed
report for each incident using the Micro Accident Analysis Package Proforma (MAAP) through field
formations and forward it to NHMP Headquarters. These accidents are periodically reviewed and
analyzed at the central level, enabling NHMP to accurately identify the underlying causes. The
findings are then utilized to formulate and implement targeted accident reduction strategies and
standard operating procedures (SOPs) aimed at minimizing the risk of future accidents.

National Transport Research Centre (NTRC) Ministry of Communications has conducted
comprehensive study and analyzed 5 year accident data to determine the causes and patterns of road
traffic accidents on National Highways and Motorways. The study established that driver behavior-
related factors, particularly careless driving are the most prominent causes of accidents on both

14

national highways and motorways contributing approximately 49% of reported cases on motorways
and 41% on National highways. In terms of collision patterns, nose-to-tail (rear-end) collisions have
been identified as the most common collision type constituting approximately 56% of accidents on
motorways and around 49% on national highways indicating issues related to driver alertness,
following distance, and speed management.

(b) On motorways, vehicle-related factors such as tyre bursts (14%) and mechanical faults
(12%) also significant, followed by over-speeding (9%) and poor road conditions (5%), with roll-over
accidents 29.6% being the second most frequent collision type. On national highways, over-speeding,
improper pedestrian crossings, and mechanical faults each contribute around 9% of accidents, while
dangerous overtaking (6%), poor road conditions (5%), and improper U-turns (4%) play smaller roles.
Collision patterns on national highways include roll-over accidents (20.8%), pedestrian-involved
accidents (10.9%), and sideswipe collisions (6.6%), with other factors contributing marginally to total
reported accidents.
The accident data for the year 2025 (up to November) also reflects a similar pattern, wherein
driver behavior-related factors such as careless driving, sudden lane changing, wrong overtaking,
improper U-turns, distracted driving (cell phone etc.), sharp cutting and failure to maintain a safe
following distance, collectively account for approximately 51.6% of reported accidents.

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Communications be pleased to state:
a) the Government's response to Central Monitoring Unit (CMU) findings that
National Highway Authority (NHA) accumulated losses reached Rs.2.074 trillion
by June 2025, with Rs1.004 trillion added in three years, and outstanding loans
stand Rs.3.1 trillion with annual debt accretion of Rs300 billion; and

b) how the Ministry justifies that despite all income doubling to Rs.64.4 billion,
finding costs soared to Rs.210 Billion in FY 25-highest among SOEs with
depreciation of Rs.133.8 Billion and finance costs of Rs.193.5 Billion eroding
profitability; and

c) what restructuring plan exists to transition NHA away from its structural deficit
requiring continuous budget support?
questions.reply:
(a) The National Highway
Authority (NHA) is a statutory body corporate established through an Act of Parliament in 1991. Its
core mandate is to ensure the delivery of an efficient, reliable, safe, and environmentally sustainable
national highway network across the country. Since its inception, NHA has played a pivotal role in
developing and maintaining the road infrastructure that supports economic growth, regional
connectivity, and national mobility.
A notable strength of NHA's institutional framework is its ability to finance a substantial
portion of its managerial and operational expenses from its own internally generated resources. This
self-sustaining financial model reduces dependence on the Federal Government for routine
expenditures and helps avoid placing additional fiscal pressure on the national budget. As a result,
NHA continues to operate with a degree of financial autonomy uncommon among many public-sector
entities.
Over the years, NHA has demonstrated steady and consistent growth in revenue generation
through a diversified portfolio of income streams. These include toll operations, right-of-way (ROW)
charges, rental income, police fines, and receipts from build-operate-transfer (BOT) projects. After
meeting operational and administrative costs, these revenue streams continue to generate positive net
cash inflows, reflecting the Authority's strong operational viability and sound revenue management.
In addition to its own revenues, the Federal Government extends annual development support
to NHA through the Public Sector Development Program (PSD) in the form of a Cash Development
Loan (CDL), provided at a government-prescribed mark-up rate. This funding mechanism is
specifically intended to support infrastructure expansion and strategic development initiatives rather
than day-to-day operations, enabling NHA to undertake large-scale national projects of economic
importance.
Despite positive operational cash flows, the reported deficit position largely stems from non-
cash accounting adjustments rather than actual financial distress. These include finance costs on PSDP
and foreign-relented loans, exchange losses on foreign relented loans, and depreciation charges. Such
items represent book entries instead of tangible cash outflows. Consequently, the accumulated losses
amounting to Rs. 2.067 trillion as of June 30, 2025 primarily reflect accounting treatment of long-term
liabilities and asset depreciation, rather than real-term cash losses, indicating that NHA remains
financially stable from an operational cash perspective. The year wise analysis of accumulated deficit
reported by NHA is given below:

(b) Despite NHA's total income doubling to Rs. 64.4 billion, the sharp rise in the reported
funding cost during the financial year 2025-the highest among SOEs - does not indicate deterioration
in operational performance.
Rather, this increase primarily reflects the accounting impact of financing large-scale
infrastructure assets through long-term borrowings, in the shape of PSP Cash Development Loans
(CDL) and foreign re-lented loans accumulated over multiple years for strategic national highway
development. As these liabilities have expanded in line with the growth of the motorway and highway
network, the corresponding finance cost of Rs. 193 billion has also risen significantly due to mark-up
accruals and exchange-rate adjustments on foreign loans.
Similarly, the depreciation charge of Rs. 133.8 billion is a non-cash accounting expense arising
from the capitalization of an extensive and continuously expanding road asset base. Since NHA
manages long-gestation infrastructure assets of national importance, higher depreciation is a natural
consequence of commissioning new highways, bridges, and motorway sections. These charges reduce
reported profitability under accounting standards but do not represent actual cash outflows in the year.
Therefore, the erosion in accounting profitability is largely attributable to non-cash depreciation
and accrued finance costs, rather than weakness in revenue generation or cash operations. In fact, the
doubling of income demonstrates improved operational efficiency and stronger monetization of tolls,
ROW, BOT, and other recurring revenue streams. The Ministry's position is that NHA remains

19

operationally cash-positive, while the reported losses mainly reflect the financial reporting treatment of
long-term infrastructure financing obligations and asset depreciation associated with a capital-intensive
public sector mandate.

(c) The following steps have already been taken to address the issue of accrual of finance
cost on Cash Development Loans and Foreign relented Loans and to achieve the financial
sustainability of NHA:
February 12, 2021: Ministry of Communications, as approved by Economic Coordination
Committee (ECC), on February 2021 notified the following sub-committee to review the progress of
NHA's Business Plan:
a) Deputy Chairman, Planning Commission Chairman
b) Secretary, Finance Division Member
c) Secretary, Economic Affair Division, Islamabad Member
d) Secretary, Ministry of Communications Member
e) Chairman, National Highway Authority, Islamabad Secretary
Pursuant to the directives of the ECC, a Business Plan was prepared through the Consultant of
Asian Development Bank (ADB) on the following parameters:
Update of existing Business Plan with revised financials and data.
Formulate and design strategies/ options to pay off liabilities and to make NHA self-
sustainable.
Prepare a comprehensive Business Plan (in shape of report) for submission to the committee &
Finance Division.
Revision of Business Plan, if required, after getting feedback from the steering committee
(already notified for the Business Plan) & Finance Division (the key stakeholder).
NHA through Ministry of Communications forwarded the Business Plan to the committee
constituted by ECC to review it and for onward submission to ECC for soliciting approval of Business
Plan.
The following proposals were part of the Business Plan:
i. Write-off the Debt as expenditure already incurred as Public Service Obligations (PSO).
ii. Share of profit from the receipts of issuance of Sukuk Bond using the underlying assets
of NHA from GOP.
iii. Equitize the debt, making GoP a shareholder in NHA.
iv. Lease-back: Exchange physical assets for debt, then lease them back.
v. Exchange excess land for debt.
vi. Repay the debt over time.
However, after detail deliberations, and after soliciting input from the Finance Division, a
revised Business Plan has already been submitted through Ministry of Communication for soliciting
approval of Economic Coordination Committee.

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Energy (Petroleum Division) be pleased to state the reasons for the
extreme reduction in Gas pressure during the load-shedding hours pressure in Sindh
province and in particular Karachi?
questions.reply:
SSGC is facing a sustained gas
shortfall primarily due to the natural depletion of indigenous gas reservoirs. Since FY 2015-16, overall
gas supplies have declined by approximately 49 percent.
In line with the load management plan approved by the Government, the Domestic,
Commercial, and Process Industrial sectors remain on top priority. However, to manage system
constraints and maintain adequate line pack, scheduled night-time gas closure and pressure profiling is
implemented in the domestic sector from 10:00 PM to 05:00 AM. This measure is necessary to ensure
sufficient gas availability during peak cooking hours. Apart from this arrangement, there is no gas load
shedding in SSGC’s franchise area, particularly for domestic consumers.

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Energy (Petroleum Division) be pleased to state:
a) whether it is a fact that the recent surge in petrol and diesel prices has fueled
inflation, increased the cost of essential goods, raised transportation expenses, and
have also placed additional financial burden on households;

b) whether it is also a fact that the sectors, such as industry and agriculture are also
adversely affected;

c) what specific measures being adopted to reduce petrol and diesel prices provide
the immediate relief to citizens, promote fuel efficient and alternative energy
solutions, encourage energy conservation; and

d) what steps are being taken to implement long-term strategies to reduce reliance on
imported petroleum while ensuring a sustainable and affordable energy supply for
the country?
questions.reply:
(a) Petroleum products
especially diesel is linked with the mass transit (human and food supply chain) and agriculture,
therefore, increase in prices of petrol and diesel has direct impact on the supply of essential goods,
transportation expenses and financial burden on household.

(b) Yes, as detailed above.

(c) Government has taken a number of steps, as briefed below, to minimize the impact of
rising prices of petroleum products on the consumers:

23

i. The price differential on petrol and diesel was provided by government for three weeks
amounting to Rs. 129 billion.
ii. The Petroleum Levy on petrol has been reduced by Rs. 80/L.
iii. Direct Fuel Subsidy to Motorcycles (Two Wheelers), Trucks, Buses and vans is being
implemented. Moreover, in case of energy conservation, government has issued directives for
work from home, lower speed limit on Motorways and early closure of markets. Furthermore,
government has been promoting the use of EVs, to replace traditional vehicles as alternative
energy solution.

(d) Government is endeavoring to expand indigenous exploration of oil and gas as well as
enhance the capacity of local refineries and encourage investors to invest in new refineries.
Government has also approved National EV policy, which aims to reduce reliance on petroleum
products.

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Energy (Petroleum Division) be pleased to state:
a) whether Petroleum Concession Agreements (PCAs), and Exploration Licenses
(ELs) were signed on February 26, 2026 for the eight blocks in the Balochistan,
two in Sindh, and one in Punjab and awarded to a joint venture comprising Oil
and Gas Development Company Limited (OGDCL), PPl, Mari Energies, Pakistan
Oil Limited (POL) and Prime Energies, with Mari Energies operating six blocks
and OGDCL operating three; and

b) whether the successful bidders have committed a minimum investment of $31
Million (Rs.8.66 Billion) over the last three years for the exploration activities, plus
Rs.276 Million for social welfare initiatives in concession areas; and

c) what specific targets exist for seismic surveys, exploratory drilling, and potential
production timelines to translate this investment into reduced import dependence?
questions.reply:
(a) Yes, 11 Petroleum
Concession Agreements (PCAs) and Exploration Licences (ELs) were executed on 26th February 2026
for eleven blocks eight in Balochistan, two in Sindh, and one in Punjab. M/s Mari Energies Limited is
the operator of six blocks, Oil and Gas Development Company Limited (OGDCL) is operating three
blocks, while Pakistan Petroleum Limited (PPL) and Pakistan Oilfields Limited (POL) are operators of
one block each.
(b) Yes, the successful bidders have committed a minimum investment of USD 31 million
(approximately Rs. 8.66 billion) over a three-year period for exploration activities, along with USD
990,000 (approximately Rs. 276 million) allocated for social welfare initiatives in the concession areas.
(c) The successful bidders for each block are required to undertake comprehensive seismic
surveys (2D/3D) and/or gravity and magnetic studies in accordance with their firm work commitments
during the initial exploration phase, typically spanning three years. These surveys are aimed at
acquiring high-quality subsurface data to accurately delineate prospective hydrocarbon-bearing
structures and identify drillable prospects. Based on the acquired data, the companies are obligated to

24
drill exploratory wells to test the identified prospects. The number and depth of wells are governed by
the minimum work commitments agreed under the respective Petroleum Concession Agreements
(PCAs) and Exploration Licenses (ELs). As described in point B.
Further in case of a commercial hydrocarbon discovery, the operators are required to promptly
proceed towards appraisal and development phases, including installation of necessary production
facilities, and initiation of production within timelines approved by the regulator. The timely execution
of these exploration and development activities is expected to enhance indigenous oil and gas
production, thereby contributing to reduction in reliance on imported energy resources and
strengthening the country’s energy security.
Furthermore, strict monitoring mechanisms are in place to ensure compliance with the agreed
work programme. And in case of default or non-fulfillment of commitments, the companies are liable
to pay Liquidated Damages (LDs) as per the applicable contractual and regulatory framework,
ensuring accountability and protection of Government interests.
