questions.question:
Will the Minister for Energy (Petroleum Division) be pleased to state:
a) why has Oil and Gas Development Company Limited (OGDCL) despite holding
the largest exploration acreage and receiving substantial public investment,
experienced a persistent decline oil and gas production and profitability over the
past five years;

b) what action has been taken to address declining out put from mature fields, and
why have these failed to deliver measurable results;

c) why has the progress on newer discoveries remained limited, and what technical,
regulatory, or managerial failures are impeding timely development;

d) whether any performance audit or restructuring has been conducted in response
to OGDC's weakening core business, especially amid falling non-operating income;

e) how does the Ministry justify OGDCL's expansion into high risk projects like
Reko Diq and Abu Dhabi Offshore block-5 without first addressing core
operational inefficiencies; and

f) what guarantees exist that newly awarded blocks under the 2025 round will
not face the same delays and underutilization, as in previous cycles?
questions.reply:
(a)

Company Profile:
The Company was established in 1961 as a Public Sector Corporation. It was converted to a
Public Limited Company in October 1997. OGDC made its debut on the Pakistan Stock Exchange in
October 2003, while its Global Depository Shares were listed on the London Stock Exchange in
December 2006. As of 30 June 2025, GOP is the majority shareholder and owns 85.02% of the
Company. It is pertinent to mention that OGDC is a self-financed and profitable entity and manages its
exploration, development and production activities through self-generated funds.
Market Share:
OGDC is the market leader in the E&P sector of the Country in terms of highest exploration
acreage, oil and gas reserves and production output in the Country. As of 31 March 2026, Company’s
exploration acreage stood at 98,311 sq. km representing 40% of the Country’s total area under
exploration. Production contribution by the Company during the 1 st half of Financial Year 2025-26
stood around 50%, 27% and 32% of Country’s total oil, natural gas and LPG production respectively.
As of 30th June 2025, Company’s reserves constitute 49.2% and 30.3% of national oil and gas reserves
respectively. Source: PPIS – Pakistan Petroleum Information Service
Historical Performance - Production and Profitability:
Despite the adverse impact of forced production curtailments by SNGPL and Uch Power
Limited (UPL), coupled with the natural decline in mature producing fields, OGDC has maintained
steady production output over the past five years (2020–21 to 2024–25). This has been achieved
through the drilling of 36 exploratory wells and 29 development wells, the discovery of 26 new
reservoirs, and the integration of 48 new wells into the production gathering system. In addition,
OGDC has undertaken extensive work overs and implemented production augmentation measures,
including the deployment of modern artificial lift systems. As a result of these efforts, Company’s
production potential has increased to 40,000 BPD oil, 865 MMSCFD gas, and 815 metric tons of LPG.
However, sales remained lower due to forced curtailment.

The CAGR during fiscal years 2020-21 to 2024-25 reflects decline of 4%, 7% and 5% for
crude oil, gas and LPG production respectively, whereas overall industry trends of country depict 8%
to 10% annual decline. However, it may be mentioned that the CAGR of OGDC production would
have been even better if there had been no force curtailment by SNGPL and UPL. Profitability for the
same period reflects positive CAGR of 17%. During the last five years OGDC has contributed Rs
1,112 billion towards national exchequer on account of corporate taxes, dividends, royalty and
government levies. Besides, Company’s oil and gas production also rendered significant foreign
exchange savings as imports substitution. Notwithstanding operational challenges, OGDC is actively
pursuing enhanced exploration, field optimization, and cost efficiency measures to stabilize production
and improve financial performance over the medium to long term. During the current fiscal year 2025-
26, OGDC's sustained efforts to assess and unlock the hydrocarbon potential in its exploratory blocks
yielded 8 oil and gas discoveries viz., Chakar-1, Bitrism East-1, Baragzai X-1 (Kingraili formation),
Baragzai X-1 (Datta formation), Baragzai X-1 (Samanasuk/Shinawari formation, Baragzai X-1
(Hangu/Lumshiwal formation), Baragzai X-1 (Lockhart formation), and Sahito-1. The combined daily
crude oil and gas production potential of these discoveries is 14,435 barrels and 76 MMcf,

29

respectively. The Company’s Reserves Replacement Ratio (RRR) for 2025-26 is expected to be around
162%, reflecting longevity in its operations, and creating long-term value for the shareholders.

(b) In order to address the phenomenon of natural decline and to optimize mature fields,
OGDC’s management took a strategic initiative in 2023 by constituting a dedicated working group on
production optimization. A five-year optimization plan finalized in 2023 is currently under
implementation which has yielded very encouraging results. Some of the initiatives are summarized as
under: - • Deployment of artificial lift systems, i.e. Electrical Submersible Pumps • Plants up-gradation
and facilities debottlenecking to enhance production. • Remedial work overs and recompletion with rig
to revive shut-in wells • Rig less interventions including re-perforations, stimulations, water shut-of
Initiation of studies through globally renowned consultants for mature fields to improve recovery
factor by drilling new development wells. • Tight gas exploitation plan formulated and under
implementation. One well has already been injected in the system. Four wells to be re-entered for tight
gas potential during FY 2025-26. • Pakistan’s first Shale Gas Pilot Project also in progress. First phase
of vertical franking successfully completed while second phase is at advanced stage of designing and
planning. • Monetization of stranded and marginal fields being pursed on fast track basis. • Jhal Magsi
field injected into system in August 2025 • Commissioning of Dakhni Compression Project in January,
2026 • Work in progress for Dhodak and Jandran fields. • 2D and 3D seismic surveys have been
conducted in mature fields - Uch, Loti, Nashpa, Nim, Tando Allah Yar, Bitrisim, Khewari, Thal, and
Missa Keswal. Additionally, surveys are planned for Pirkoh, Zin, Sinjhoro, Wali, and Betani fields.
Ongoing studies aim to evaluate further upside potential and are expected to enhance the production
profile of these fields. • Revitalization plan for Bobi Field (District Sanghar) prepared that includes one
exploratory well and one development well. Necessary study is currently underway. • Augmentation of
Sinjhoro Gas Field (District Sanghar) for enhancement of production capacity from 50 mmscfd to 90
mmscfd is currently under implementation. • Flagship program of Rajian Field “District Chakwal” is in
progress. 11 shut-in/depleted wells to be re-entered / recompleted besides drilling of new development
well. During the last five years oil production from the field has been increased from 1500 bbl/d to
4500 bbl/d and it is aimed to enhance it further up to 14000 bbl/d by December 2027. • Revival of
Missa Keswal field in Tehsil Gujar Khan has been planned. Locations of 2 new wells have been
marked, land acquisition under section 4 is in progress.

Monetization of Low BTU Zin Block District Dera Bugti is under discussion with Government
of Balochistan and private sector. Furthermore, 480 L.km Seismic planned to explore potential of three
new structures. Since March 2023, the above listed production optimization measures have resulted in
additional volume of 5,300,000 bbls oil, 35,100 mmscf gas and 30,000 M.ton LPG. Looking ahead,
OGDC geared up to sustain this momentum through the implementation of additional artificial lift
technologies, compression projects, drilling of new infill wells, along with sustainability projects
including pressure maintenance and enhanced oil recovery (EOR) techniques.
(c) OGDC typically operates in geographically and geologically challenging terrains and
subsurface structures. These challenges exacerbate due to security issues. Notwithstanding aforesaid
position, focus always remains on fast-track monetization of discoveries. Establishment of Bettani
early production facility is a testament to Company’s fast track monetization strategy. Discovery made
in July 2021 in security sensitive district of Laki Marwat was commercialized in June 2023. However,
those discoveries which were marginal or stranded or of low pressure or low BTU and therefore could
not be connected to the national transmission system have been offered through an open competitive
process for 3rd party sales listed at Annexure-A. Pakistan’s upstream petroleum sector; operates under
a well defined and mature regulatory framework. The relationship of the Government with upstream
petroleum companies is governed under policies issued from time to time and the Petroleum
Concession Agreements. Exploratory work on onshore blocks has witnessed some challenges on

30

account of security issues. OGDC, however, has maintained closer engagement with law enforcement
agencies for the continuation of its operations on the production and exploration fronts. None of
OGDC’s producing fields at this stage is non-operational due to security issues, Exploratory work,
however, can be accelerated in few blocks if security clearance is granted.

(d) OGDC is a publicly listed company and has well-entrenched corporate governance
framework. Operational, financial and strategic performance of the Company is discussed and
evaluated by its Board every quarter. The Company has an independent audit function which reports
directly to the Audit Committee of the Board. Targets, performance and achievements of the Company
are appraised and evaluated by the Board annually on the basis of Key Performance Indicator (KPIs)
already set for the year. The Company engaged world class external auditors M/s A.F. Ferguson & Co.
and M/s KPMG Taseer Hadi & Co. for its audit related functions. The Company is also being advised
by Wood Mackenzie on its strategy and investment in Pakistan’s offshore. Furthermore, on the
directives of Public Accounts Committee, performance audit has been conducted by the Auditor
General of Pakistan. As mentioned above, OGDC has successfully improved its production capability
and if the prevailing trend of forced curtailment is addressed, Company’s revenue from its core
business will further improve. It is however, to be noted that oil and gas prices are linked with
international market and therefore not insulated from global fluctuations. Non-core Income: The
Company’s non-core income during fiscal years 2020-21 to 2024-25 reflects a positive CAGR of 56%
. OGDC’s non-operating income remained a strong contributor to business financial performance.
However, given the volatile nature of interest rate/exchange rate, non-operating income is mainly
influenced by interest income on investments and bank deposits and exchange gain/loss. In order to
overcome the volatility in non-operating income as well as to boost core business income, OGDC has
proactively initiated a range of strategic and operational measures, which include: • Enhanced focus on
exploration and production activities to augment hydrocarbon reserves and sustain production levels •
Optimization of existing assets through work overs, recompletions, and improved recovery techniques
• Cost rationalization and efficiency improvement initiatives across operations • Regular review of
exploration and production portfolio to prioritize high-impact and economically viable projects •
Leveraging advanced technology, cutting-edge production techniques and improved engineering
design and simulation capabilities to minimize natural decline in the mature fields. In addition to the
above, the Company is actively pursuing a continuous improvement approach through targeted
interventions and strategic realignment to address emerging business challenges and enhance long-
term sustainability. OGDC remains committed towards improving upstream performance and
contributing to national energy security through prudent financial management and operational
excellence.
(e) Investment in Reko Diq is compatible with Company’s diversification strategy.
OGDC’s joint venture with Barrick Gold Corporation for the development of one of the largest copper
and gold deposits in the world is a flagship investment which will ensure a steady and sustainable
revenue stream for OGDC, local partners and the province of Balochistan. Copper is one of the key
elements in the global energy transition landscape. Feasibility study has been completed and
development work at site is in full swing and procurement of most of the long lead items has also been
completed; manufacturing of the machinery and equipment is progressing ahead. As a result of
investment in Reko Diq, OGDC has diversified in the mineral and mining sector without
compromising its core business. OGDC’s investment in Abu Dhabi offshore block 5 along with
Pakistan Petroleum Limited (PPL), Mari Energies Limited (MEL) and Government Holding Private
Limited (GHPL) is a joint venture between the Pakistani companies and ADNOC (National Oil
Company of Abu Dhabi). On the basis of progress made by Pakistani consortium, ADNOC exercised
its right to obtain 60% shareholding in the block. For all future expenditures, the Pakistani consortium
will be responsible for 40% while for remaining 60%, ADNOC will contribute its share. Field
development plan has been approved by ADNOC and monetization is expected during 2028.

31

(f) Formal award of blocks pursuant to the 2025 bidding round is being finalized by the
DGPC. OGDC meanwhile has developed a strategy for exploratory activities and the committed work
program. The Company has allocated resources to undertake exploratory work in its exploration
licenses subject to security clearance. In order to fast track exploration work, OGDC not only utilizes
its five seismic crews but also outsources the exploration work.

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Energy (Power Division) be pleased to state:
a) the rationale behind the recent changes in the net metering policy;

b) whether the Government intends to provide protection or grandfathering to
existing net metering consumers;

c) what measures are being taken by the Government to restore investor confidence
and encourage renewable energy adoption; and

d) whether the Government plans to review or revise the policy in consultation with
stakeholders?
questions.reply:
(a) Under
the previous net metering framework, prosumers were able to avoid fixed charges associated with
the capacity installed to meet their electricity demand. As a result, non-net metering consumers
effectively bore additional costs to compensate for these avoided charges.
The transition from net metering to a net billing mechanism under the Prosumers Regulations
addresses this imbalance by ensuring that prosumers contribute appropriately toward fixed and
capacity-related costs. This shift reduces cross-subsidization and promotes a more equitable
allocation of costs across all categories of consumers.

(b) Existing consumers shall remain protected under the Prosumers Regulations until the
expiry of their license period. Upon completion of this term, they will transition to the revised policy
framework.

(c) Pakistan’s net metering policy has played a key role in promoting distributed solar
energy, enabling households and businesses to reduce reliance on the grid and support cleaner
energy initiatives.
The new Prosumers Regulations does not stop consumers to install distributed generation and
instead approx. 8000 MW has been made committed in the IGCEP while promoting the renewable
energy adoption in the country.

(d) NEPRA has conducted a public hearing in a transparent manner before changing the
regulations where all facts and figures were placed in front of the regulator as well as the public.
Furthermore, a detailed consultative session was also conducted before revision of the prosumer
regulation by the NEPRA. Furthermore, the existing consumers are already safeguarded from the
revised policy.

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Communications be pleased to state:
a) whether the Ministry has taken any action to relocate or design highways that
cause urban congestion or encroach heritage zones; and

b) the names of such projects under review or design?
questions.reply:
(a) The Government of Pakistan is
committed to strengthening connectivity across the country through the development of new
transportation infrastructure, while also implementing appropriate measures to improve existing
networks and alleviate urban congestion.
• Highways attract traffic by making travel faster and more convenient, encouraging
greater use by people and businesses. Over time, this enhanced accessibility increases
the value of adjacent land and stimulates economic activity. Commercial, residential,
and industrial developments emerge along these corridors to take advantage of
improved connectivity. Consequently, highways evolve into economic hubs, driving
urban expansion and increasing population density along their routes. Highways
themselves do not encroach nearby heritage zones. However, rapid urbanization and
economic activities and poor oversight by local administration may affect the nearby
heritage zones.

36

• To manage this urbanization and the associated traffic congestion, the Government of
Pakistan adopts a two-pronged approach subject to availability of funds. First, new
bypasses are constructed to divert traffic away from urban centers, thereby reducing
pressure on city roads and improving travel efficiency. Second, existing highways are
systematically widened and upgraded to accommodate higher traffic volumes through
increased lane capacity, improved junction design, and enhanced traffic management
systems. Together, these measures help alleviate congestion while promoting more
balanced and sustainable development. This process entails development of detailed
design, Engineer’s Estimates, and Bill of Quantities based on National Highway
Authority (NHA)’s Composite Schedule of Rates (CSR).

(b) To this end, some of the projects are highlighted below: -
 Widening and improvement of 330 Km Indus Highway N-55, under Central Asian
Regional Economic Corridor (CAREC) Tranche-I and II, with the financial assistance
of Asian Development Bank (ADB) wherein multiple new bypasses are constructed.
 Widening and improvement of 48 Km section of National Highway N-45 from
Kalkatak to Chitral is in “procurement of contractor” phase.
 Widening and improvement of 39 Km section of National Highway N-45 from
Chakdara to Timergara is in “PC-I approval” phase, and design has already been
completed.
 Government of Pakistan is also actively working towards realization of Hyderabad –
Sukkur Motorway project, which will alleviate traffic congestion on existing National
Highway N-5 besides providing a high-speed traffic facility. Design has already been
completed, and three packages are in “procurement of contractor” phase.
 Reconstruction of different sections (total length approx. 210 Km) of National Highway
N-5 across Sindh, Punjab, and KP provinces under Pakistan’s Resilient Recovery,
Rehabilitation, and Reconstruction Framework Project, with the financial assistance of
Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB), China.

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Foreign Affairs be pleased to state:
a) whether it is a fact that apostille documents are no longer physically attested at the
Ministry; if so, since when and under what policy;
b) whether the attestation process has been outsourced to private courier companies such as
TCS, Leopards, and Gerry's; if so, the reasons and terms thereof;
c) whether it is also a fact that the required postal ticket is available only at one post office,
causing long queues; if so, the reasons thereof;
d) whether the Government plans to expand this facility to multiple post offices; if so, the timeline
thereof; and
e) whether the Ministry intends to increase attestation counters or introduce an
online/appointment system to address public difficulties?
questions.reply:
(a) The Ministry of Foreign
Affairs (MOFA) facilitates apostille attestation through three designated channels:
1. Walk-In Submissions
Reserved for legal documents and Powers of Attorney as well as any cases requiring biometric
verification (e.g., business documents). All walk-in applicants are attended to on the same day,
regardless of volume. Additionally, applicants with urgent deadlines such as scholarships or

42
confirmed travel bookings are prioritized upon verification of supporting documents, which are
retained for official records.
Walk-in access is restricted to these categories due to capacity constraints. MOFA currently
processes approximately 8,000–9,000 documents per day with a staff of 16 officials. Given the
sensitivity and scrutiny required for each attestation, unrestricted walk-in access would
significantly exceed operational capacity and compromise attestation standards.
2. Online Appointments
For all documents other than legal documents, applicants are required to book an online
appointment. Upon scheduling, applicants visit the attestation hall in person to submit their
documents, which are attested on the same day.
3. Courier Submissions
Applicants may submit documents through registered courier companies. The courier
representatives submit the documents physically to the attestation team, where they are processed
by the apostille staff and returned to the courier for delivery back to the applicant.
MOFA is currently processing apostille attestations across all three channels, operating at and
often beyond full capacity. This is being achieved within existing manpower and resource
constraints, while maintaining the integrity and procedural standards of the attestation.
b) The Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) has not outsourced the attestation process to
private entities. However, to facilitate applicants who are unable to visit MOFA or its Camp
Offices (Lahore, Karachi, Gujrat, Peshawar, and Quetta), particularly those residing in remote
areas or with personal constraints; an alternative submission channel has been provided through
designated courier services, namely TCS, Leopards, and Gerry’s.
These courier companies only collect documents from applicants and forward them to
MOFA or its liaison offices for processing. The attestation is carried out exclusively by MOFA
or its Camp Offices. Upon completion, the attested documents are returned to applicants via the
same courier services.
c) Apostille attestation does not require a post ticket. Its fee is paid online after document
verification or deposited in the bank, including for walk-in appointments. In contrast, General
attestation requires a post ticket, which can be purchased from the post office located adjacent to
the Consular Hall of the Foreign Office.
Most applicants purchase the post ticket before submitting their documents at the
Consular Section. The general perception that applicants wait for hours is incorrect; the average
waiting time is between 2 and 20 minutes, even during peak hours.
d) The post office may be advised to make post tickets available at major GPOs or other
branches for public convenience. However, based on applicant feedback, most prefer to use the
Foreign Office post office as it offers a nearby, one-stop facility.
e) Regarding increasing number of attestation counters, the existing Consular Hall,
established in 2013, can no longer accommodate the growing number of applicants for general
and apostille attestations. To address this, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs has approved the

43
construction of a new attestation building within the Foreign Office premises. The site has been
finalized, and consultations are underway regarding its design. The project is expected to take
approximately six-seven years to complete, after which the number of service counters will be
significantly increased to meet the rising public demand of attestation.
An appointment-based system is already in place for Apostille attestation, through
which approximately 250–300 applicants are facilitated daily, in addition to walk-in and courier
submissions.
The Ministry is also undertaking the transition of general attestation from a manual to
an online system. In this regard, the National Information Technology Board (NITB), which
developed the Apostille online portal, has been tasked with establishing a similar online
appointment mechanism for general attestation to efficiently accommodate requests from the
public.

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Energy (Power Division) be pleased to state:
a) whether it is a fact that Government has amended billing mechanism for net-metered solar
consumer, including declaring excess electricity as zero units in certain cases; if so, the details
and rationale thereof; and
b) whether it is also a fact that financial incentives for surplus electricity generation and relief
based on Export Maximum Demand Indicator (MDI) readings have been withdrawn for
consumers exceeding approved capacity; if so, the reasons thereof?
questions.reply:
(a) As per
the Prosumers Regulations, the billing mechanism has been revised for new consumers by
transitioning from net metering to a net billing arrangement. However, existing net-metered
consumers remain protected under the current regime until the expiry of their licenses, and the
prevailing mechanism including buyback at the NEPRA-determined Power Purchase Price (PPP)
continues to apply. There is no provision of declaring excess electricity as zero units. However,
where a consumer installs Distributed Generation (DG) capacity beyond the approved limit under
the net-metering agreement, any generation above the sanctioned capacity is not accounted for, as
that constitutes a violation of the contractual terms.
(b) Yes, the financial incentive for surplus electricity exported beyond the approved
Distributed Generation (DG) capacity during any billing month has been restricted up to the
approved DG capacity for that specific month. This restriction applies in cases where the installed
DG capacity exceeds the limits approved under the net-metering concurrence, constituting a
violation of the approved capacity.

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Foreign Affairs be pleased to state:
a) the types of attestation services provided by the Ministry along with the
procedure for attestation of each type of document attested by the Ministry;

b) whether the Ministry has taken notice of their difficulties faced by the general
public, including queues, overcrowding, and hours of waiting, due to the
absence of round the clock attestation services in attestation centers;
c) whether the Ministry intends to introduce a comprehensive online appointment
system for both normal and urgent attestation of all types of documents for
ordinary attestation as same as apostille attestation and the time period
required for its implementation; and

d) the steps being taken by the Ministry to simplify attestation procedure,
introduction of evening shift or round the clock attestation services?
questions.reply:
(a) The Ministry of
Foreign Affairs provides the following types of attestation services:

a. Appostille attestation (for Hague Convention countries)
 Applicant submits original document along with a copy.
 Prior verification from relevant issuing authority (e.g. IBCC, HEC, NADRA, Chamber of
Commerce) is mandatory.
 Documents are submitted at designated counters or through authorized courier services.
b. General Attestation (for non-Hague Convention countries)
 Original documents must be pre-attested by concerned authorities.
 Documents are submitted at MoFA Camp Offices or headquarters.
 After scrutiny, attestation stamps is affixed.
c. Attestation of Commercial Documents
 Documents must be verified by relevant Chambers of Commerce.
 Submission through company representative.
 Attestation is carried out after due verification.
d. Attestation through Courier Services
 Applicants may submit documents via authorized courier companies.
 Courier ensures collection, submission and return delivery after attestation.
Procedure (General)
 Prior attestation/verification from relevant authority.
 Submission at MoFA offices or through courier.
 Token issuance and processing.
 Scrutiny and verification
 Attestation/appostille and return to applicant.
Procedure (Appostille)
 Applicant submits original documents through online appointment
 After verification, appostille sticker is affixed.

(b) The Ministry is fully cognizant of the difficulties being faced by the general public at
attestation centers, including long queues, overcrowding, and extended waiting hours. These
challenges have been noted through public feedback, administrative reports, and periodic reviews
conducted to assess service delivery standards.
In response, the Ministry has undertaken a series of measures aimed at improving efficiency
and facilitating applicants. Efforts are being made to enhance operational capacity by increasing the
number of counters, streamlining verification procedures, and deploying additional staff during
peak hours. Furthermore, the introduction and expansion of online appointment systems have been
prioritized to reduce walk-in congestion and ensure a more organized flow of applicants.
The matter of providing round-the-clock attestation services is also under active
consideration. While certain logistical and administrative constraints exist, the Ministry is exploring
feasible options to extend service hours in a phased manner. Pilot initiatives may be introduced to
evaluate the effectiveness of extended hours before broader implementation.
The Ministry remains committed to improving public service delivery and ensuring that
attestation services are accessible, efficient, and citizen-friendly. Continuous monitoring and
feedback mechanisms are being strengthened to addressed public concerns promptly and to further
enhance the overall experience of applicants.

(c) With regard to the introduction of a comprehensive online appointment system, the
ministry has already initiated steps towards digitization and automation of attestation services. An
online appointment facility for certain categories of documents has been introduced and is being
progressively expanded. The Ministry is working to integrate both ordinary and urgent attestation

6

services, including appostille-related processes where applicable, into a unified digital platform.
The timeline for full implementation is being finalized, keeping in view technical, operational, and
security considerations.

(d) The Ministry has undertaken several steps to simplify and improve attestation
services, including:
 Streamlining verification procedures with relevant authorities
 Enhancing coordination with courier services
 Increasing processing counters to reduce waiting time
 Public facilitation through guidance and awareness measures
Furthermore, evening shift services have been introduced at Asaan Khidmat Markaz, where
attestation-related facilitation is available from 8:00 AM to 8:00 PM, significantly improving public
access and reducing congestion during peak hours.

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Energy (Power Division) be pleased to state:
a) whether it is a fact that, in order to upgrade the power infrastructure and
ensure un-interrupted electricity supply including the replacement of broken or
damaged electricity poles and the up-gradation of overloaded transformers, in
Umeed Garh, Tehsil Kabirwala, District Khanewal, the required instruments
and equipment were mobilized and shifted to the aforesaid village, but were
later retrieved without execution of the planned works;

b) if so, the reasons for the retrieval of the equipment and the delay in execution of
the said proposal;
c) whether it is a also a fact a new survey has been conducted; if so, the details
thereof;

d) whether the Ministry intends to take any corrective or remedial measures to
ensure timely implementation of the project; and

e) what steps are being taken by the government to improve the overall power
infrastructure in Umeed Garh and the surrounding areas and to prevent
further inconvenience to the public?

Minister for Energy (Power Division) (Sardar Awais Ahmad Khan Leghari) (a) Yes.
A Low-Tension (LT) Proposal for improvement of electricity infrastructure in Umeed Garh,
Tehsil Kabirwala, District Khanewal was approved vide Work Order No. 45-159001 and issued
to Project Director (Construction), MEPCO on dated 22.07.2025. Materials were accordingly
allocated on 18.08.2025 and drawn by the line staff. However, upon mobilization of execution
team on 25.08.2025, resistance from some local inhabitants hindered commencement of works.
Subsequently, the works could not be executed.

(b) The execution team of RRE (Renovation & Rural Electrification) Formation was
prevented from carrying out works due to local dispute and resistance at site. In view of continued
hindrance and dispute, XEN (Construction) MEPCO Division Khanewal requested cancellation of
the LT proposal vide letter dated 26.11.2025. The previously drawn material was returned to
Regional Store, Multan vide Material Return Note (MRN) No. 2181/11 dated 24.10.2025.

(c) Now on the request of inhabitants of Umeed Garh, Construction formation Khanewal
has conducted revised survey of the LT proposal on 09.03.2026.

(d) As stated in part (c), a new survey has recently been conducted. Following
completion of the estimation process, the case will be processed accordingly, and the work is
expected to be completed within six months, subject to the availability of budget and materials,
and provided that no Right of Way (RoW) issues arise to hinder progress.

(e) DISCOs undertake periodic system reinforcement, pole replacement, transformer
capacity enhancement and loss reduction measures under its annual maintenance and system
improvement plans. Further proposals for strengthening the distribution network in Umeed Garh
and adjoining localities shall be considered subject to amicable resolution of local hindrances
and availability of budgetary allocation.

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Energy (Petroleum Division) be pleased to state what action has
been taken against companies involved in under invoicing or hoarding of petroleum
products?
questions.reply:
(a) Right from the start of
the crisis in March 2026, all the movement of Petroleum products are maintained on daily basis.
Pakistan as a country has performed in a better way compare to the whole of this region and has
been successful in maintaining the oil supply chain in the country. The product is available across

13
the country at retail outlets, however, OGRA alongwith the Ministry of Energy and other
institutions is strictly observing the oil supply in the country.
In a proactive approach, to avoid any chance of product hoarding, OGRA took following
actions:
i. OGRA has issued Show Cause Notices to seventeen Oil Marketing Companies
(OMCs) over observed variances between planned & actual sales.
ii. OGRA in coordination with Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) and Intelligence
Bureau (IB), conducted nationwide field inspections from March 27–31, 2026 inter
alia including 135 oil depots of OMCs, 5 refinery storages, and 15 third-party storage
facilities at Port Qasim and Keamari terminals to physically verify inventory.
iii. In addition to above, OGRA has requested all provincial Chief Secretaries alongwith
request to direct all Deputy Commissioners to undertake regular inspections and take
prompt and strict action against the entities involved in such illegal hoarding, under
the applicable provisions of Prevention of Profiteering and Hoarding Act.

Will the Minister for Energy (Power Division) be pleased to state:
a) whether there exists any policy of the Islamabad Electric Supply Company regarding
provision of separate electricity connections/meters for multiple commercial units, shops
situated within a single building in the rural areas;
b) what are the prescribed requirements procedures and eligibility criteria for obtaining
ten separate electricity meters for ten shops in one premises;
c) whether any restrictions, additional charges or load limitations are applicable in such
cases; and
d) what is the average time required for processing and installation of such connections?
questions.reply:
(a)
IESCO allows provision of separate electricity connection/ meters for multiple commercial units
and shops situated in a single building including in rural areas subject to compliance with
prevailing rules/ regulations mentioned in NEPRA Consumer Service Manual (CSM) 2025.

(b) Application seeking multiple connections for shops within 01 premises are
required to submit documents as per NERPA CSM 2025 Clauses 2.2 & 2.3 (Annex-A). Load
assessment shall be carried out in accordance with the Consumer Service Manual (CSM) of
National Electric Power Regulatory Authority. In cases where adequate spare capacity is
available on the existing distribution transformer, the electricity connection shall be provided
therefrom. However, where the available capacity is found to be insufficient to cater to the
applied load, installation of a dedicated transformer shall be proposed to ensure safe and
reliable supply. After approval of external electrification and its completion the following
process shall be followed for individual connections:

 Separate applications for each shop.
 Pay Demand Notice for the payment of Capital cost and Security amount

(c) Provision of connections are subject to fulfillment of guidelines mentioned in
Clause 2.6.3 of NEPRA CSM 2025 (Annex-B) wherein the consolidated load up to 15 kW is fed
through common distribution transformer subject to the availability of load. However, for 15 kW
to 100 kW load the dedicated transformer or transformer sharing charges proportionate to load
will be recovered from the sponsor. The rehabilitation charges on actual basis (if any) will also
be recovered from the sponsor. The sponsor will also be required to deposit 50% Grid Sharing
charges @ Rs. 4474/ kW, if the building is above ground Plus 03 stories.
(d) As per Annex-III of NEPRA CSM 2025 (Annex-C) for category - 1 up to 15 kW
the time for processing / installation of new connection is 30 days and for connection above 15
kW but not exceeding 70 kW the time for processing / installation of new connection is 44 days.
(Annexures have been placed in the National Assembly Library)

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Poverty Alleviation and Social Safety be
pleased to state the details of the arrangement for Ramzan
Packages by the Federal Government in the absence of Utility
Stores Corporations (USC) for Hyderabad and other cities of the
country?
questions.reply:
Prime Minister’s Ramzan Relief Package (PMRRP) 2026
has been approved with a total financial allocation of PKR 38 billion,
building upon the successful implementation of last year’s Ramzan cash
assistance initiative. The package aims to provide targeted relief to the
poorest and most vulnerable households through direct cash transfers,
using data from the National Socio-Economic Registry (NSER) to ensure
transparency, accurate targeting, and effective delivery.

A one-time cash assistance of PKR 13,000 is being provided to
approximately 2.1 million families with NSER scores ranging between 32
and 36. These households fall just above the eligibility threshold of the
unconditional cash transfer program and remain economically vulnerable.

Secondly, an additional allocation of PKR 10 billion has been
approved to support nearly 10 million families who are already
beneficiaries of existing government cash assistance initiatives,
strengthening their purchasing power during Ramzan.

BENAZIR INCOME SUPPORT PROGRAMMEE (BISP)

2
The Prime Minister’s Ramzan Relief Package (PMRRP) 2026 was
announced by the Federal Government with the approval of Cabinet.
Under the programme, an amount of Rs. 13,000/- per beneficiary family
was disbursed to around 1.9 million families across the country. The
Program was implemented through coordinated efforts of Ministry of
Poverty Alleviation Social Safety (Mo PA	SS), State Bank of Pakistan
(SBP), BISP, NADRA, M/o Information and Broadcasting, M/o
Information Technology, PTA, NTC, telecom operators, and partner
financial institutions, ensuring transparent beneficiary verification, direct
payments, and nationwide outreach through SMS alerts, robocalls and a
centralized call center. Te role of BISP was related to provision of
National Socio-Economic Registry (NSER) database as per approved
parameters and also coordination with SBP.

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Climate Change and Environmental
Coordination be pleased to state:

(a) whether the Federal Government has assessed the growing
threat of chemical pollution in the country, particularly its
implications on the public health, food safety and the
environment;

(b) whether it is a fact the Federal Government organizations are
responsible for monitoring, regulation and enforcement
relating to industrial and agricultural chemicals, including
their coordination mechanisms;

(c) whether any national levels audit or inventory of hazardous
chemicals has been conducted to evaluate contamination of
soil, water or food sources; if so, the details thereof;

(d) the steps taken by the Government to update Federal toxicity
and labeling standards in line with international conventions;
and

(e) the details of Federal initiatives underway to raise awareness,
promote safe chemical handling and support adoption of

sustainable and non-toxic alternatives across industries and
agriculture?
questions.reply:
(a) The Ministry of Climate Change
and Environmental Coordination (MoCC	EC) is under process of
developing a Draft National Integrated Chemical Management and
Safety Framework after assessment of industrial chemical pollution and
its impacts on human health and environment.

Additionally, both federal and provincial Environmental Protection
Agencies had already formulated regulations on hazardous substances
under their respective Environmental Protection Acts.

(b) At the national level, monitoring, regulation, and enforcement
of industrial and agricultural chemicals is implemented by relevant
institutions as under:

1. Ministry of Climate Change Environmental
Coordination (MoCC	EC) leads national policy
development on transboundary movement and safe disposal
of chemicals and hazardous waste, coordinates
implementation of multilateral environmental agreements
(Basel, Rotterdam, Stockholm, Minamata, and GFC), which
provides overall national guidance. For the transboundary
control of hazardous waste and chemicals, MoCC	EC
follows the Prior Informed Consent (PIC) procedure that
requires international exporters to share details about
potentially hazardous chemical shipments to Pakistan.
Further, importers seeking to import restricted waste are
required to apply for NOCs through the respective Provincial
EPAs. Applications are evaluated in accordance with the
SOPs aligned with the Basel Convention before issuance of
approvals. This allows Pakistan to carry out detailed risk
assessment and make a decision, protecting national
environment and public health.
2. Pakistan Environmental Protection Agency (Pak- EPA)
enforces environmental regulations at the federal level,
including controls on hazardous substances, emissions,
effluents, and waste management under the Pakistan
Environmental Protection Act, 1997.

5

3. Provincial Environmental Protection Agencies (EPAs) are
responsible for monitoring and enforcement within their
jurisdictions under their respective Environmental Protection
Acts.

4. Ministry of National Food Security Research (MNFSR)
regulates agricultural chemicals, including pesticides,
fertilizers, and related inputs, through bodies such as the
Department of Plant Protection (DPP) and the Federal
Seed Certification Registration Department
(FSC	RD).

5. Other Ministries and departments, like the Ministry of
Industries Production (MoIP) Pakistan Customs / Federal
Board of Revenue (FBR), and Ministry of Interior also
oversee matters related to chemicals, such as industrial
operations and standards related to chemical production and
use, import and export controls for chemicals, licensing for
control of chemicals and precursors used in products, etc.

Coordination Mechanisms

x MoCC	EC facilitates federal-provincial coordination on
policy, implementation, and reporting to Multilateral
Environmental Agreements (MEAs).

x Technical Working Groups under various international
conventions (Basel, Rotterdam, Stockholm, Minamata) ensure
inter-agency coordination on specific chemical streams.

x Customs-EPA coordination platforms support information
sharing for import/export control of regulated chemicals.

(c) MoCC	EC has prepared a detailed inventory of hazardous
chemicals that are persistent in nature (known as forever chemicals, or
POPs) as part of its National Implementation Plan (NIP) to the
Stockholm Convention, a copy of which is available on MoCC	EC
website at:

https://chm.pops.int/Portals/0/download.aspx?d UNEP-POPS-NIP-
Pakistan-COP4.English.pdf

6

Also, the Pakistan Council of Research on Water Resources
(PCRWR) has carried out a detailed assessment of hazardous chemicals,
including Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs) contamination in surface
water, groundwater, and sediments. The report is available on PCRWR
website at:

https://pcrwr.gov.pk/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/Monitoring-of-
Persistent- Organic-Pollutants-in-Hydrosphere-of-Pakistan-2022.pdf
Furthermore, the control and regulation of chemical pollution in
the agriculture sector is regulated by the Plant Protection Department of
Ministry of National Food Security Research.

Additionally, the Ministry of Climate Change Environmental
Coordination has also conducted the country’s first-generation hazardous
waste inventory, covering key sectors including textiles, healthcare,
shipbreaking, and others.

(d) MoCC	EC has developed toxicity and labeling standards for
chemicals in Pakistan as per international best practices for safe handling,
use, and trade of hazardous substances it the Draft Globally Harmonized
System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals (Annex-I).

(e) The Ministry of Climate Change Environmental
Coordination (MoCC	EC) has undertaken several initiatives:

1. Capacity Building and Training Programs:

x Several workshops and training sessions have conducted for
industry, agricultural stakeholders, and enforcement agencies
to promote safe handling, storage, and disposal of chemicals
including POPs.

x Technical sessions conducted for industries on minimizing
chemical risks and implementing best practices.

2. National Frameworks and Action Plans:

x The National Integrated Chemical Management and Safety
Framework which guides awareness-raising, chemical safety
practices, and adoption of non-toxic alternatives.

7
x Adoption of the GHS plan will help standardize toxicity
classification and labeling, supporting safe handling across
sectors.

3. Promotion of Sustainable and Non-Toxic Alternatives:

x Projects under the Framework encourage substitution of
hazardous chemicals with safer and environment-friendly
alternatives in industries and agriculture.
x Alternative green chemicals will be provided to some textile
industries to facilitate transition to green technologies and
chemicals.

(Annexure has been placed in the National Assembly Library).

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Information Technology and
Telecommunication be pleased to state:

(a) whether the Government has installed or upgraded a national
internet filtering or monitoring system, including the Web
Monitoring System (WMS) or any related firewall
infrastructure in Pakistan; if so, the details thereof;

(b) the total cost incurred on procurement, installation and
maintenance of such systems since 2018;

(c) the names of companies or vendors contracted for supplying
this technology and whether the contracts are available for
public or parliamentary scrutiny;

(d) whether the Government has conducted any assessment
regarding reported slowdown of internet services and its
impact on freelancers, IT companies and digital businesses;
and

(e) what safeguards exist to ensure these systems are not used for
unlawful surveillance, censorship or violations of citizens
constitutional rights including freedom of expression and
privacy?
questions.reply:
(a) Since 2007, WMS in one form or
another has been deployed by the Telecom Operators in compliance of
their license obligation. WMS is procured and funded by the Operators
without utilization of any public money. Details are as under:

x In 2007, upon direction of PTA, a technical System was
deployed by LDIs licensees to curb grey telephony.
x This System termed as μITMS (International traffic
Monitoring System)’ became operational in 2008 for
monitoring and blocking of grey calls coming into the country
via internet. Owing to its positive results, it was upgraded in
2009.

x On 13th Aug 2012, pursuant to Policy Directive on ICH,
ITMS was upgraded and termed as μGrey Traffic
Monitoring System (GTMS)’.

x GTMS started operations in Oct 2013 and was capable to
identify, detect and block grey calls coming into the country.
Withdrawal of ICH policy in June 2014, ended GTMS
funding mechanism, impacting its effectiveness.

x In 2017, PTA directed the licensees to upgrade GTMS or
provide new System.

x The August Supreme Court also took suo-moto over grey
traffic and on 25th Oct, 2018 in HRC No. 72583/2018,
directed for deployment of System in next 6 months.

x New System termed as μWeb Monitoring System (WMS)’
became functional in March 2020 having capability to block
grey traffic and filter/block objectionable internet content.

x WMS is capable of:

o Mitigation of Grey traffic

o Blocking of objectionable content under PECA
(pornographic/blasphemous/anti-state etc.)

9
x WMS operations has resulted in an average increase of 100
million LDI minutes /month in 2025 compared to 2024. It
also proved useful for blocking malicious IPs and Indian
content during Pak-India escalation in 2025.

(b) It is done in collaboration with cellular mobile operators and
PTA is not involved in the procurement.

(c) As in Para (B)

(d) Pakistan’s IT sector is experiencing an unprecedented surge,
with ICT export remittances reaching $3.8 billion²in FY 2024-25
compared to $3.2 billion in FY 2023-24-an 18.5% year-on-year increase.
This growth is bolstered by a thriving community of freelancers whose
remittances have become a cornerstone of the digital economy. The
country’s rising global profile is reflected in the 2024 Global
Cybersecurity Index (GCI), where Pakistan leaped from 79th to Tier-1
(Role-Modelling) status, ranking among the top 40 nations.
Simultaneously, Pakistan improved by 14 spots in the UN E-Government
Development Index (EGDI), moving to 136th place and entering the
³High EGDI ́ category for the first time.

Improving connectivity has been one of the key driver of the IT
exports growth. Key Drivers of Pakistan’s IT Growth:

x Export Surge: In December 2025, Pakistan’s IT and IT-
enabled services exports reached a record $437 million.
marking the first time monthly receipts crossed the $400
million threshold.
x Global Recognition: Secured Tier-1 status in the GCI 2024
and jumped to 88th in the E-Participation Index, showcasing
enhanced digital governance.

x Infrastructure Reforms: The successful 5G spectrum
auction in 2026 is set to provide the ³digital highway ́ to
further booth the ICT market including IT exports. \

x Connectivity Initiatives: Extensive fiberization projects are
closing the urban-rural divide and stabilizing the internet
backbone.

10
x Freelance Ecosystem: Regulatory reforms and formal
remittance channels have enabled freelancers to contribute
significantly to the total annual remittances.

(e) Freedom of expression of views and right to privacy are
fundamental rights. These rights are not absolute rights rather constitution
itself puts reasonable limitations on the exercise of these rights. No
censorship is done to compromise these rights. However certain
cybersecurity imperatives necessitate the installation of such systems.
Further it is also done strictly in the context of controlling gray traffic.

questions.reply:

implementation of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in educational
institutions.

questions.question:
Will the Minister In-charge of the Prime Minister’s Office be
pleased to state:

has state of the art emergency response system, drone

combating natural disasters nationwide;

the loss of lives and property; and

(d) the time by which the practical steps will be taken by the
Federal Government to meet the said deficiencies?
questions.reply:
(a) 1.
NDMA has established a state-of-the-art National Emergency
Operations Centre (NEOC), which is equipped with advanced
dashboards and digital portals for monitoring, information sharing and
disaster reporting. NDMA has also developed a mobile application for
timely dissemination of early warnings to stakeholders and the general
public. In addition, NDMA maintains strategically located warehouses
across the country to mobilize emergency relief resources and support
response operations when required.

35
2. Simultaneously, PDMAs and provincial authorities have
also established their own Emergency Operations Centres, equipped
with necessary technologies and dashboards. Furthermore, all federating
units have established rescue services such as Rescue 1122 and Urban

either incorporated drone monitoring systems or are in the process of
integrating such technologies to enhance disaster monitoring and response.

(b) Gilgit-Baltistan Disaster Management Authority
(GBDMA), State Disaster Management Authority (SDMA) and ICT
Emergency Services are currently in the process of incorporating

Management Authorities (PDMAs) and provincial rescue services are

disaster surveillance and response operations at limited scale and are in
the process of enhancing these capacities.

undertaken on a continuous basis by the respective provincial authorities.

questions.question:
Will the Minister for Climate Change and Environmental
Coordination be pleased to state:

(a) the detail of the losses caused by continuous climate change
in the country during the last five years and the areas where
such losses have occurred; and

(b) the steps taken by the Government in this regard till date
alongwith the results achieved so far?
questions.reply:
(a) During the past five years, the
country has been facing recurrent climate-induced disasters, resulting in
widespread human, economic, and environmental losses.

The 2025 monsoon in Pakistan caused severe cloudbursts and
floods, particularly in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Punjab, Sindh, Gilgit-
Baltistan, and AJK, causing hundreds of deaths, displacing millions,
submerging farmland, and destroying homes and infrastructure. Extreme
downpours and flash floods overwhelmed drainage systems and prompted
large-scale evacuations, with climate change intensifying rainfall
variability and flood severity. The flood has caused an estimated 950
deaths, more than 1,000 injuries, the displacement of a million people, and
the submergence of over 4,500 villages in Punjab alone. (Source: NDMA -
Monsoon 2025 Final Consolidated Situation Report No. 87 (02-10-2025).

The 2022 floods in Pakistan affected over 33 million people,
destroyed or damaged 2.3 million houses, caused over 1,700 deaths, and
inflicted an estimated USD 30 billion in damages to infrastructure,
housing, agriculture, and the economy.

In addition to floods, glacial melting in the Hindukush-Karakoram-
Himalaya region is accelerating, threatening long-term water and food
security. Pakistan hosts 13,032 glaciers covering around 13,546 kmð.
Rising temperatures have led to the formation of glacial lakes, putting 7.1
million people at risk of Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOFS).

Sea intrusion along the Indus Delta is causing large-scale loss of
arable and habitable land. Estimates indicate that more than 3.5 million
acres of fertile land in Sindh have been degraded or lost to seawater
intrusion, displacing thousands of coastal families and threatening
mangrove ecosystems critical to fisheries and coastal protection.

37
Recurring heatwaves have intensified in recent years, with extreme
temperatures exceeding 50C in Jacobabad and Sibi, causing heatstroke
deaths, a reduction in agricultural productivity, and severe water stress.
Heatwaves in 2022 alone reportedly caused hundreds of deaths and
reduced wheat yields by an estimated 10-15% in affected districts.

Smog and air pollution episodes, especially in Lahore and central
Punjab, have worsened, with Air Quality Index (AQI) levels frequently
exceeding 400-500, leading to widespread respiratory illnesses, disruption
of daily life, and significant public health costs. The World Bank estimates
that air pollution causes annual economic losses of up to USD 6 billion in
Pakistan.

Soil erosion and land degradation, driven by erratic rainfall and
deforestation, have also intensified. Around 27% of Pakistan’s land area
faces degradation, reducing agricultural productivity and increasing
vulnerability to droughts and floods.

Overall, Pakistan suffers average annual climate-related losses
exceeding billions of dollars, alongside mounting social and ecological
costs.

For comprehensive picture of climate-induced loses, the report
provided by NDMA is attached at Annex-I. The report has given an
outlook of the affected areas viz point 3 at page 10 onwards.

Additionally, the NDMA’s flood mapping, highlighting affected
areas are also attached below:

o NDMA’s Urban Areas Flood Mapping (Annex-II)

o NDMA’s rural Areas Flood Mapping (Annex-III)

o NDMA’s Punjab Flood Mapping (Annex-IV)

o NDMA’s Sindh Flood Mapping (Annex-V)

(b) The Ministry of Climate Change Environmental
Coordination has taken several steps to address these challenges:

38
The Ministry of Climate Change Environmental Coordination
(MoCC	EC) is mandated to formulate, coordinate, and oversee national
policies and actions related to climate change, particularly climate
adaptation and resilience. It has undertaken several strategic initiatives to
guide and mainstream climate considerations into national and provincial
development planning. These include:

National Climate Change Policy 2021²updated to align national
priorities with emerging climate challenges.

National Adaptation Plan 2023²a comprehensive plan to guide
climate-resilient development pathways.

Nationally Determined Contributions ² supporting mitigation
and adaptation actions in line with global commitments.

Monsoon 2026 Strategic Plan: Approved by the PM in November
2025, the Plan delineates short, medium, and long-term goals for flood
preparedness, resilience, and recovery mechanisms.

Framework for Implementation of Climate Change Policy
(2014-2030) a roadmap for sectoral climate actions across the country.

National Communication on Climate Change²reporting
progress and commitments under the United Nations Framework
Convention on Climate Change.

Mainstreaming gender considerations in all climate action
programs.

MoCC	EC is also working to strengthen institutional
coordination, enhance climate finance access, build provincial capacity,
and promote research, awareness, and early warning systems to deal with
evolving climate risks.

Major National Climate Initiatives

To respond to these challenges, several ongoing and planned
initiatives offer scalable models:

39
SAFER Project (by MoCC	EC and International Center for
Integrated Mountain Development, funded by Adaptation Fund): focuses
on integrated watershed management, nature-based recharge systems,
wetlands rehabilitation, climate-resilient WASH systems, cryosphere risk
management, and early warning systems across Gilgit-Baltistan, Khyber
Pakhtunkhwa, and Sindh aligning with the National Adaptation Plan and
Living Indus Initiative.

The GIZ-funded Strengthening Climate Adaptation and
Resilience (SAR) project in Pakistan (2021-2025) supports the
government in enhancing climate resilience through risk assessments,
planning, and financing. It focuses on building the capacity of public and
private partners to implement climate adaptation measures in sectors like
agriculture, water, and health.

Upscaling Green Pakistan Program (UGPP): builds on the Ten
Billion Tree Tsunami Program to finance check dams, sediment traps, and
forest landscape restoration through Public Sector Development Program
funding.

Buner and Shangla Early Warning Project (by World Food
Program): installs hydromet stations, river monitoring, and community-
based early warning systems in glacier-prone mountainous areas.

District Adaptation Plans/Locally Led Adaptation Plans: In
order to bolster the resilience of the vulnerable communities, district
adaptation plans are in process.

Coordination with the Provinces: The Ministry keeps liaison
with the provinces, issues advisories, and engages them in capacity-
building and training, under the umbrella of Nǹȇ.

The outcomes of the initiatives taken by MoCC	EC are as follow:

40

41

42

Apart from the MoCC	EC’s initiatives, the NDMA has prepared
the National Disaster Response Plan (NDRP) 2026 which is framed to
provide a comprehensive, coordinated and scalable framework for disaster
response across Pakistan. It serves as a blueprint for national and regional
authorities, humanitarian partners, private sector and civil society to work
in concert in mitigating losses, protecting lives and livelihoods and driving
resilient recovery in the face of natural and human-induced hazards.
Consequently, the P	Ds and PDMAs are responsible for consolidating
damage assessments and recovery strategies. The major share of
expenditure on rehabilitation and reconstruction is being financed through
the Public Sector Development Programme (PSDP), supplemented by
allocations from the Finance Division to key institutions such as the
National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) and the Benazir
Income Support Programme (BISP). Additionally, resources under the
Annual Development Programme (ADP) also contribute to recovery
efforts at provincial and local levels.

The Economic Affairs Division (EAD) plays a crucial role in
coordinating with international development partners, particularly the
World Bank (WB) and the Asian Development Bank (ADB), to facilitate
the repurposing and reallocation of existing loans toward post-disaster
recovery and resilience-building initiatives.

The Ministry of Climate Change (MoCC) does not maintain
comprehensive data on all aspects of post-disaster interventions. Instead,

43
the Finance Division, EAD, NDMA and provincial P	D departments are
in a stronger position to provide detailed, consolidated, and up-to-date
information regarding financial allocations, project implementation, and
overall post-disaster recovery efforts.

(Annexures have been placed in the National Assembly Library).

questions.question:
Will the Minister In-Charge of the Special Investment Facilitation
Council be pleased to state:

(a) why profit repatriation surged 27.92% to 1.7 billion dollars in
July to January, 2025-26 despite the Special Investment
Facilitation Council (SIFC) claims of restored investor
confidence with 442.76 million dollars outflows to UK linked
investors and 413.11 million dollars to China linked
companies representing capital flight rather than retained
reinvestment;

(b) whether the energy sector recorded 400.19 million dollars
and financial services 371.33 million dollars in profit
remittances; and

(c) what concrete reinvestment conditions exist in SIFC
facilitated agreements with Gulf countries to ensure
investments translate into long term productive assets rather
than short term profit extraction?
questions.reply:
(a) The Investment Policy of Pakistan 2023 (PIP 2023),
approved by the federal cabinet, explicitly guarantees foreign investors the
right to repatriate profits, capital, and dividends. The investment policy in
vogue provides a level playing field and does not discriminate between a
local and foreign investor.

x Foreign investors in any sector may repatriate their capital,
profits, dividends, or any other funds in the currency of their
investment or into any other freely usable currency, subject to
Foreign Exchange Regulations of the State Bank of Pakistan
and provisions of the Companies Act 2017. Remittance of

44
royalties, technical assistance fees, franchise fees, cross
charges, transfer pricing and business process outsourcing
related payments are allowed subject to the rules/regulations
and procedural requirements set under the Foreign Exchange
Manual of the State Bank of Pakistan.

x The reported increase of 27.92% in profit repatriation to USD
1.7 billion during July-January FY2025-26 does not signify
capital flight, but rather reflects a normalization of external
payment flows and improved investor confidence. During the
preceding period, profit repatriation had been partially
constrained due to foreign exchange management measures;
the current rise indicates the easing of these restrictions by the
State Bank of Pakistan, enabling legitimate and pending profit
remittances to be cleared.

x A significant portion of the outflows to the United Kingdom
(USD 442.76 million) and China (USD 413.11 million)
corresponds to repatriation by established foreign investors
operating in sectors such as energy, financial services, and
telecommunications. These remittances are consistent with
contractual obligations and do not represent disinvestment or
exit of capital. On the contrary, the ability to repatriate profits
is a key determinant of investor confidence and is viewed
positively by international investors.

x Furthermore, data indicates continued foreign investment activity,
reinvestment of earnings, and sustained operational presence of
major foreign firms, particularly under facilitation mechanisms
such as the Special Investment Facilitation Council. The observed
trend therefore reflects a transition from restricted to normalized
financial flows, rather than a withdrawal of capital from the
economy.

x The Government remains committed to maintaining a balanced
framework that ensures ease of profit repatriation alongside
policies to incentivize reinvestment, including sector-specific
facilitation, regulatory streamlining, and investment protection
measures.

(b) Yes, sectoral data indicates that during July-January
FY2025-26, profit remittances were recorded at approximately

45
USD 400.19 million from the energy sector and USD 371.33 million from
financial services. These figures primarily reflect returns on investments
by foreign companies operating in power generation, oil and gas, and
banking sectors.

x Such remittances are consistent with the contractual and regulatory
framework governing foreign investment in Pakistan and are
processed in accordance with guidelines of the State Bank of
Pakistan. The outflows largely pertain to dividend payments and
profit transfers by operational entities with ongoing business
activities in the country.

x It is pertinent to note that these remittances do not indicate sectoral
decline or capital withdrawal; rather, they represent normal profit
realization by investors. Both sectors continue to attract and retain
foreign investment, supported by policy facilitation measures and
investment frameworks promoted through platforms such as the
Special Investment Facilitation Council.

(c) No specific provisions exist, however, under the internal
facilitation framework of the Special Investment Facilitation Council,
partner countries are engaged to promote long-term, asset-based
investments. While profit repatriation remains permissible in line with
Pakistan’s investment regime, the following concrete reinvestment and
retention-oriented conditions are embedded within project structuring and
facilitation mechanisms:

1. Asset-Backed Investment Structures:

Investments are predominantly directed toward brownfield
and greenfield projects (e.g., energy, mining, agriculture,
logistics, and infrastructure), ensuring capital is tied to
physical, revenue-generating assets with long gestation
periods.

2. Reinvestment Expansion Incentives:

Fiscal and regulatory incentives are structured to encourage
reinvestment of profits into capacity expansion, technology
upgradation, and downstream value addition within Pakistan.

46
3. Local Value Addition Industrial Linkages:

Projects are designed with mandatory or incentivized local
content requirements, employment generation targets, and
integration with domestic supply chains to embed long-term
economic activity.

4. Performance-Linked Concessions:

Concessions (including tax facilitation, land access, and
regulatory fast-tracking) are increasingly explored to be
embedded as performance benchmarks such as production
levels, export realization, and reinvestment milestones.

5. Joint Venture / Public-Private Partnership Models:

Many SIFC-facilitated projects adopt JV or PPP structures
with Pakistani entities, ensuring shared ownership, knowledge
transfer, and sustained local stakeholding.

6. Regulatory Oversight Monitoring:

A centralized monitoring mechanism tracks project
implementation, financial flows, and compliance with agreed
terms, ensuring alignment with national economic objectives.

7. Sector-Specific Frameworks (e.g., Mining Agriculture):
In strategic sectors, agreements include provisions for
downstream processing, value retention within Pakistan, and
restrictions on raw resource extraction without local
beneficiation.

questions.question:
Will the Minister In-Charge of the Special Investment Facilitation
Council be pleased to state the criteria used by SIFC to evaluate

questions.reply:
x Single-Window Facilitation: The SIFC operates as a ³one-
window ́ platform for investors, helping them navigate

and Provincial governments.

secretaries, evaluate sector-specific concerns and develop

x Three-Tier Governance Structure: Proposals are processed

priorities

x Executive Committee: Co-chaired by the Minister for

Will the Minister for Information Technology and
Telecommunication be pleased to state:

(a) whether the Government has approved or is implementing the
rollout of 5G services in Pakistan;

(b) the details of the proposed 5G plan including areas of initial
deployment participating telecom operators and expected
benefits for consumers and businesses;

(c) the timeline for implementation of 5G across the country; and

(d) the steps taken by the Government to ensure affordability,
accessibility and cyber security of the network?
questions.reply:
(a) Yes, GoP issued Policy Directive for
the Next Generation Mobile Services (NGMS)/5G spectrum auction on
6th January 2026. Accordingly, the spectrum auction was conducted on
10th and 12th March 2026 in order to enhance 4G Quality of Service
(QoS) and to launch of 5G services in the country. All CMOS actively
participated in the auction and collectively secured an additional.

49

480 MHz of spectrum, increasing their total spectrum holdings
from 274 MHz to 754 MHz.

Subsequently, PTA granted NGMS/5G licenses to PMCL (Jazz),
PTML (Ufone), and CMPak (Zong) on 19th March 2026, enabling CMOs
to commence the deployment and rollout of 5G services across the
country.

(b) The licenses issued after recent NGMS/5G spectrum auction
includes enhanced targets for rollout and QoS obligations. It obligates
CMOs to deploy at least 1,000 4G/5G sites per year. 4G sites shall be
proportionately distributed between urban and rural areas in each province
whereas 5G rollout prioritizes Federal and Provincial capitals, including
Islamabad, Karachi, Lahore, Peshawar, and Quetta, in the first phase, with
subsequent expansion to other major cities. CMOs are in process of
procuring/ import of equipment to establish new 4G/5G sites and a visible
enhancement in coverage/QoS is expected in next 4 to 6 months.

New 4G sites will enhance network performance and QoS by
increasing capacity and reducing congestion. Furthermore, 5G rollout will
deliver higher data speeds, lower latency, and improved reliability,
enabling advanced services such as lot, smart cities, e-health, and e-
education, and supporting overall digital transformation and economic
growth in Pakistan.

(c) As per the issued licenses, CMOs are required to deploy at
least 1,000 4G/5G sites per year, and the implementation of 5G across
Pakistan will be carried out in following four phases:

i. Phase 1 (2026-2028): 5G Launch in Federal and Provincial
capitals i.e Islamabad, Rawalpindi, Karachi, Lahore,
Peshawar, and Quetta.

ii. Phase 2 (2028-2030): 5G expansion to 10 x additional cities
(at least 2x cities from each province) and key locations,
including universities, industrial zones, airports, hospitals, and
transit hubs.

iii. Phase 3 (2030-2032): Further 5G rollout in 10 x additional
cities (at least 2 x cities from each province) and hotspots
coverage. to enhance

50

iv. Phase 4 (2032-2035): 5G rollout in 15 x additional cities (at
least 2 x cities from each province).

Furthermore, enhanced Quality of Service (QoS) thresholds are
also incorporated in said licenses, data rate for 4G has been enhanced from
4 Mbps to 20 Mbps, with a further increase to 50 Mbps in a phased
manner. For 5G, data rate of 50 Mbps has been introduced, with an end-
state target of 100 Mbps in phased manner to ensure significantly
improved network performance and user experience.

(d) The Government of Pakistan and PTA have undertaken a
range of policy, regulatory, and consultative measures to ensure
affordability of 5G services. In this regard, a flexible and investor-friendly
spectrum pricing framework has been adopted, comprising reasonable
reserve prices, a one-year moratorium, and extended payment tenures.
These measures are aimed at reducing the upfront financial burden on
operators, enabling cost-efficient network rollout and, ultimately,
affordable services for consumers. PTA is also promoting infrastructure
sharing, including passive and active sharing, to reduce capital and
operational costs and facilitate efficient network deployment.

PTA continues to foster a competitive and investment-friendly
regulatory are environment to support affordable service offerings. Under
the Mobile Tariff Regulations, 2025, the Authority regulates tariffs to
prevent excessive pricing and anti-competitive behavior, and retains the
power to intervene where consumer interests are adversely affected.
Relevant operators required to obtain prior approvals for tariff revisions in
line with regulatory provisions, while all operators must ensure
transparency through publication of tariffs to enable informed consumer
choice. Currently, 5G services are being offered within existing data
packages without additional charges. PTA also conducts regular
